{"stdout":"# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. AI-enabled intrusions and malware, fraud and scams, deepfakes, influence operations, surveillance, prompt injection and agent exploits, model theft / illicit distillation, bio/chem misuse reports; procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies.
- **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. Clinical results, FDA/Health Canada/WHO actions, drug discovery, AI for science, biosecurity; legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings and filings, government reports, standards — US federal and state, EU, UK, Canada, China, international bodies.

**Subagent return format** — one block per item, then a short list of rejected candidates and why:

```
SECTION: <one of the eight section names>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)
```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Use only what the returned text actually says; if it comes back as a paywall stub, a login page or nothing usable, fall back to search-result text or another source and say in the bullet where the figures came from. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

## 3. Write the edition — `data/DATE.json`

Schema (see `data/2026-09-11.json` for a full example once it exists):

```json
{
  "date": "YYYY-MM-DD",
  "edition": "daily",
  "generated_at": "<ISO-8601 UTC timestamp>",
  "window": "e.g. 10 Sep 11:00 → 11 Sep 11:00 UTC",
  "title": "The episode's name — 3 to 10 words, a statement: who did what, or what changed. No period, no colon, no figure that is not in the summary. It is read in podcast apps as 'Name [2 Oct 2026]', so it must stand alone.",
  "summary": ["paragraph 1", "paragraph 2"],
  "sections": [
    {
      "name": "<one of the eight section names below>",
      "items": [
        {
          "headline": "Specific, factual, one line — who did what, with the key number",
          "sources": [{ "name": "Anthropic", "url": "https://..." }, { "name": "Reuters", "url": "https://..." }],
          "bullets": ["What was announced/found, with numbers.", "Why it matters / what it changes.", "Caveats, what is unverified, what to watch."],
          "topics": ["anthropic", "threat-intel", "cyber-offense"],
          "storylines": ["ai-enabled-hacking"],
          "impact": "beneficial" | "harmful" | "mixed" | "neutral",
          "flags": ["company-claim" | "single-source" | "preprint" | "update"]
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Section names** (exactly these; omit a section if it has nothing that day):
1. `Frontier models & labs` — releases, capabilities, benchmarks, lab announcements, safety cases, system cards.
2. `Research & papers` — papers with results: new methods, evals, interpretability, alignment, scaling. State the result and the number.
3. `Security, misuse & threat intelligence` — threat-intel reports, documented attacks using AI, influence operations, scams/deepfakes, model vulnerabilities, prompt injection, jailbreaks, agent security.
4. `Military, defense & geopolitics` — procurement, deployment, autonomous weapons, export controls, national strategies, China/US/EU competition.
5. `Health, science & medicine` — clinical results, FDA actions, drug discovery, AI-for-science results, hospital deployments and their measured outcomes.
6. `Policy, regulation & law` — legislation, regulation, enforcement, court rulings, government reports, standards.
7. `Compute, chips & infrastructure` — chips, fabs, datacenters, power, capex figures, funding rounds and deals with numbers.
8. `Deployment & impact` — large-scale rollouts, labor effects, measured societal effects, incidents, the good and the bad in practice.

**Summary**: 2–3 paragraphs, ~150–250 words. The three to five things that matter most today, stated as facts, with the numbers. No throat-clearing, no "in today's edition".

**Headlines**: one line, specific, factual. "Anthropic report: Russian state group GTG-20006 used Claude to automate espionage against Ukrainian and European governments" — not "Anthropic releases threat report".

**Bullets**: 2–4 per item. First bullet is the fact with the number. Then significance. Then caveats — say plainly what is unverified, what the source did not say, what to watch. Write in complete sentences. Never pad.

**Sources**: 1–4 per item, primary first. `name` is the publisher (Anthropic, arXiv, Reuters, FDA, Court docket), not the article title.

**Topics**: 1–4 lowercase-hyphen slugs per item. Reuse existing slugs (`node scripts/build.js --topics`). Canonical slugs to prefer: `anthropic`, `openai`, `google-deepmind`, `meta`, `xai`, `mistral`, `deepseek`, `qwen`, `nvidia`, `microsoft`, `amazon`, `apple`, `threat-intel`, `cyber-offense`, `cyber-defense`, `influence-ops`, `scams-fraud`, `deepfakes`, `prompt-injection`, `agents`, `agent-security`, `alignment`, `interpretability`, `evals`, `open-weights`, `reasoning-models`, `scaling`, `compute`, `chips`, `export-controls`, `energy`, `datacenters`, `china`, `eu-ai-act`, `us-federal-policy`, `us-state-policy`, `uk`, `copyright`, `privacy`, `military`, `autonomous-weapons`, `pentagon`, `healthcare`, `fda`, `drug-discovery`, `bio-risk`, `ai-for-science`, `robotics`, `labor`, `education`, `elections`, `surveillance`, `child-safety`, `incidents`, `funding`, `earnings`. Add an entity slug (company, agency, named group) when the story is about that entity.

**Storylines** (optional; usually one, at most two): the ids from `node scripts/build.js --storylines` whose arc this item advances — a new development in *that story*, not merely the same topic. Only existing ids with status `live` or `proposed`; the validator rejects unknown or resolved ids. Omit the key when the item belongs to none. Never coin an id here.

**Impact** (optional but encouraged): `beneficial`, `harmful`, `mixed`, or `neutral` — the demonstrated effect in the story, not your prediction.

**Flags** (include every one that applies; omit the key if none): `company-claim` — a company-reported benchmark, user count, revenue or capability claim not independently verified; `single-source` — only one outlet has it; `preprint` — research not peer reviewed; `update` — a story covered in an earlier edition, with new facts only.

**Style**: plain, declarative, numbers over adjectives. Attribute claims ("Anthropic says", "the paper reports", "according to the filing"). No hype, no hedging language beyond what the sources support. British or American spelling — either, consistently.

FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)

# Claude Opus 5.5

September 22, 2026

Scroll down

We’re introducing Claude Opus 5.5, the first model in our new Claude 5.5 family. It performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on most work and costs 40% less to run than Opus 5.
Claude Opus 5.5 is our first release since we called for pacing the frontier . It was tested before release by external evaluators, including Frontier Design and METR . On our automated behavioral audit, the most comprehensive alignment test we run, Opus 5.5 is the strongest-performing model we’ve tested to date. It also comes with the safeguards we’ve developed for our most capable models.
Here are some of the improvements you can expect from Opus 5.5:
Performance. Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5. It’s the new leading model, and early testers saw large jumps in performance on their most complex work. One tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day—work that would have taken an engineering team weeks. It’s good at finding and fixing inefficiencies in software: when we asked it to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times, while Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also altered the app’s behavior. A different tester had several Claude models build a game from a single prompt; Opus 5.5 scored higher than any other model on the strength of its graphics and polish.
Safety. Opus 5.5 achieves the best scores of any model to date on our automated behavioral audit, our alignment suite that tests Claude across thousands of simulated scenarios. It is much less likely than recent models to take hard-to-reverse actions or act outside the boundaries it’s been given, and it’s more resistant than Opus 5 to prompt injection. We’ve also broadened our alignment testing to cover longer tasks, impossible tasks, and scenarios modeled on real incidents, though it still has limits. Full details of our evaluation are available in the Opus 5.5 System Card .
Because Opus 5.5 is comparable to Claude Mythos 5.1 in biology and cybersecurity, we’re deploying it with safeguards similar to those on Claude Fable 5.1. Vetted organizations can apply today to our Life Sciences Verification Program to use Opus 5.5 for biology research. In the coming weeks we will also be expanding access to our Cyber Verification Program , and verified cybersecurity practitioners will be able to use Opus 5.5 for their work.
Cost and speed. Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.
In addition to the price drop, we’re increasing five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, Team, and seat-based Enterprise plans. We’re also providing subscription users a rate limit reset, which you can now save and use whenever you choose.
Communication. Opus 5.5 communicates more naturally than prior models. Early testers found its writing clearer and easier to follow, which addresses some of the common feedback we heard about Opus 5. It puts the most important information up front, and its style makes it a better work partner over long sessions. As one early tester put it, “it writes the way I do.” In our own use, this has made Opus 5.5’s work easier to follow and check—which is a safety benefit as well as a practical one.
Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 will follow in the coming weeks, with many of the same improvements to performance, efficiency, and safety.

# Performance and cost-effectiveness
On our benchmarks, Claude Opus 5.5 leads in agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge work. The post How can we trust AI in national defense missions? appeared first on DefenseScoop . ]]> According to recent media reports , false intelligence generated by AI came close to causing a military confrontation with China this spring. Thinking a Chinese ship in the Middle East was carrying components for nuclear weapons, the U.S. military was prepared to board the vessel. Just before the operation was launched, it was discovered that a chatbot had inaccurately identified the ship’s cargo. With the Department of War (DoW) aggressively pushing to implement AI across all levels, we cannot assume that close calls like this one will be isolated incidents. What’s needed is a transparent and verified way to answer the question: How can we trust AI in national defense missions? # Two Levels of Decision-Making To answer that question, some have suggested two factors for consideration: the reversibility of the decision and its consequences. Reversible and non-consequential decisions can reside with AI, while non-reversible and highly consequential decisions should reside with the “human in the loop.” This looks and sounds reasonable, but it oversimplifies a highly complex problem. For example, if we trust AI to make all the decisions for easily reversed simple challenges, that’s ok on the micro level – but the scale of risk increases exponentially if all these lesser decisions are factored into an irrevocable high-impact decision. These lesser decisions might be low-consequence and easily reversed, but it’s a fallacy to assume the logic required to make every low-impact decision is equally simple and clear. Adding to this complexity, security questions are rarely a single input-output operation, especially in military decision-making processes involving sensor data, intelligence, and reporting, at a minimum. When AI is involved here, the process is understood in key stages: - Information Collection - Mission analysis - Course of Action (COA) Development - COA Analysis and Comparison - Decision and Orders Production - Execution and Assessment This is a dynamic process, with interconnected decisions that need to be executed at mission speed, with the expectation that all the factors leading to the final decision will need to withstand scrutiny at a future date. Amidst this backdrop, it’s easy to see how unchecked AI decision-making – even with low consequence and reversible decisions – compounds risk throughout the process, ultimately leading to bad outcomes. The decision chain for any high-stakes decision is only as strong as its weakest link. One bad decision in a chain can condition future outputs, ultimately leading the “human in the loop” to a final decision with consequences that might result in the loss of innocent life, investigations and committee hearings. You can’t evaluate what you can’t inspect. You can’t defend a decision you can’t explain. You can’t correct a failure you can’t see. And an answer you can’t trace is an answer you can’t trust. # Inaccurate and Unexplainable According to the Stanford University Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence , “AI models struggle to tell the difference between knowledge and belief,” and its new accuracy benchmark indicates that “hallucination rates across 26 top models range from 22% to 94%.” The “State of AI in 2025 – Agents, Innovation and Transformation ” report from McKinsey Consulting uncovers two glaring problems with the implementation of AI – inaccuracy and a lack of understanding where the answers are coming from: “Inaccuracy is one of two risks that most respondents say their organizations are working to mitigate. However, the second-most-commonly-reported risk— explainability—is not among the most commonly mitigated.” The entire point of using AI to support intelligence missions is to support overburdened human decision-makers so they can make better decisions faster. So, we must identify when the smaller “reversible and non-consequential” decisions can be trusted, and when further investigation is required, so that intelligence analysts can advance with confidence. Otherwise, we run a high risk of increasing cognitive load and overburdening analysts at a time when lives are at risk. For the next eight months, the unit will incorporate the Oculus-based NeuroTrainer into their flight-training regimen, to measure whether pilots’ reaction times improve.

“In the 101st Combat Aviation Brigade, our pilots operate in unpredictable environments where split-second decisions dictate mission success,” Col. Anthony Marston, the unit’s commander, told Defense One. “By putting our aviators through the targeted exercises using the NeuroTrainer, we want to see if it can measurably improve their processing abilities.”

Pilots will do three headset sessions a week, playing two games for at least six minutes. One game requires them to catch orange balls while dodging projectiles, and the other challenges them to identify a robot teammate outside of their immediate field of view, then swat a ball in that teammate’s direction.

“All the VR-based exercises are designed to challenge and improve reaction time, situational awareness, and quick-decision making,” said Capt. Drew Lightsey, a spokesman for the 101st CAB.

During the initial phase of the program, unit pilots will do a round on the NeuroTrainer and then get in a helicopter simulator to measure their cognition, a news release said.  

“It had a little bit of a learning curve to start,” said Chief Warrant Officer 2 Eric Low, a CH-47 Chinook maintenance test pilot. “Once you start to get the hang of it, it felt like a video game. I like how it challenged different aspects of hand-eye coordination and the ability to track multiple objects at the same time.”

The second phase begins at week 15, when 70 pilots will be evaluated on their long-term results.

“Evaluators will consider the speed at which aircrews perform emergency procedures in the simulator and a qualitative assessment asking open-ended survey questions on how participants felt they improved after using the system over time,” Lightsey said.

Down the line, the NeuroTrainer could become a tool for pilots to use on days when they aren’t flying, or for staff pilots who don’t fly frequently but need to keep their skills sharp.

“I think this device could bring awareness to some of the underlying issues affecting our pilots,” said Victor Rodriguez, cognitive performance specialist for the 101st CAB’s Holistic Health and Fitness program. “The performance results could help us recognize when to discuss stress, oversaturation, or emotional regulation with them to help them improve.”

The press release said that similar headset tests are taking place at Navy Fighter Weapons School, Air Force Special Operations Command, and the 75th Ranger Regiment.

https://www.404media.co/ https://www.404media.co/favicon.png 404 Media https://www.404media.co/ Ghost 6.74 Sat, 31 Oct 2026 11:00:11 GMT 60 https://www.404media.co/people-used-to-drink-wine-made-from-ground-up-mummies-now-scientists-are-studying-it/ 6ae4de6acc39c20001bc818f Sat, 31 Oct 2026 11:00:00 GMT

Welcome back to the Abstract—and Happy Halloween! Here are the studies this week that smashed into Earth, put aliens on ice, drank mummy wine, and hugged it out.
First, a century-old theory that comets enriched Earth with the stuff of life is upended by new models of ancient impacts. Then: the case for life in extraterrestrial sea ice, a Halloween-coded medieval concoction, and a scientific embrace.
As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter The BeX Files .

# Did the seeds of life come from above or below?
Anslow, Richard J. et al. “Cometary impacts are an unlikely pathway towards the origins of life on Earth.” Scientific Reports.
Carl Sagan eloquently said that we are all made of “star stuff,” but just how much of us is really comet vomit? This is a hotly debated question in science due to the popular theory that comets delivered essential ingredients for life to Earth during impacts more than four billion years ago, paving the way for the curious emergence of Earthlings.
But scientists have thrown cold primordial water on this idea in a new study that challenges “the long-held assumption that cometary impacts played an important role in the origins of life on Earth.” By running more than 100,000 advanced simulations of comet impacts, the team found that key prebiotic molecules found in comets, such as hydrogen cyanide, would be smashed to smithereens during impacts with Earth’s ancient surface in most cases.
Moreover, while Earth was pummeled by these snowballs during its youth—relatable!—this bombardment doesn’t neatly line up with the timeline of abiogenesis, the term of the origin of life. For these reasons, it’s much more likely that life assembled from earthly molecules that leaked out from our planet’s interior, according to the study.
“The most probable timing of successful cometary impact is in the early Hadean…more than 100 [million years] earlier than the estimated emergence of the last universal common ancestor (LUCA) at 4.2 [billion years ago],” said researchers led by Richard Anslow of the University of Cambridge.
“Taken together, the rapid decline in Earth’s cometary impact bombardment and the efficient destruction of fragile cometary organics indicate that the successful delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules was an exceedingly rare event,” the team added.
The researchers didn’t rule out the possibility altogether, but concluded that any impact that had a direct influence on abiogenesis would be an edge case. That said, comets might serve as prebiotic wellsprings on other planets, such as Mars, where key molecules might have faced better odds of survival upon impact due to the red planet's smaller mass and thin atmosphere.
“Mars would have been the more favourable target for the cometary delivery of prebiotic feedstock molecules” which “strengthens the possibility that life could have emerged on Mars,” the study concluded.
In other news…

# The tip of an alien iceberg
Barrier, Edouard et al “Sea Ice as an Origin of Life Location for Hycean and Ocean Worlds.” Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society.
While we’re on the topic of prebiotic feedstock molecules—a household conversation, no doubt—let’s speculate about their accumulation on weird exoplanets. In a new study, scientists suggest that these molecules might build up in sea ice on a variety of extraterrestrial ocean worlds, providing a pathway to the emergence of aliens.
“Water worlds with potential deep oceans are at the forefront of currently observable exoplanetary habitability,” said researchers led by Edouard Barrier of the University of Cambridge. “Here we outline a location where nutrients could be concentrated in sufficiently high quantities to make abiogenesis possible—at the interface between the open ocean and the surface ice shelf.”
Concept art of a Hycean planet. Image: Pablo Carlos Budassi
The team studied the dynamics of sea ice on Earth, and modelled how similar features might form on a range of different exoplanets, including hypothetical “Hycean” planets. These are worlds more massive than Earth, but smaller than Neptune, making them part of the “sub-Neptune” class of exoplanets.
The results revealed mechanisms that “may plausibly provide concentrated chemical feedstock for prebiotic chemistry” on many of these exoplanets, suggesting they could be a substrate for the emergence of alien life. This “rich avenue of research…has the potential to significantly advance our understanding of aquaplanet habitability, and particularly to improve the prospects of abiogenesis on sub-Neptunes,” the team concluded.
What a week for the prebiotic feedstock beat! Taken together, these studies point to multiple onramps for life on worlds like Earth, Mars, exotic sub-Neptunes, and more, upping odds that life exists elsewhere in the universe—regardless of whether we ever find it.

# Drink the mummy wine
Berger, Tim, and Naimi, Amira et al.“New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
To celebrate Halloween, here’s a trick and a treat all wrapped up in one delightfully grotesque story about mummies. Roughly 700 years ago, someone had the interesting idea of grinding up parts of Egyptian mummies, mixing the residue with wine or other liquids, and prescribing it as a medicinal elixir for people to drink.
This resulting product, known as Mumia vera aegyptiaca , circulated in Arabic and European markets for centuries, but its exact composition and pharmacology remain unclear. You know what that means: It’s time to do science on the medieval mummy cocktails.
Two historic apothecary vessels of Mumia vera from Hamburg Museum (left) and Deutsches Apothekenmuseum Heidelberg, Germany (right). Images: Christoph Braun and Bullenwächter
Researchers analyzed historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. The team discovered a wide range of formulas for this medicine, including one powdered product that appears to have been derived from a mummified head.
The results demonstrate that “an apparently uninformative powdered material can be chemically linked to a specific mummified head,” said researchers co-led by Tim Berger and Amira Naimi of Marburg University. “This study shows that linking historical texts, material culture, molecular composition, and bioactivity, can open new routes for decoding historical medicines and reconstructing the material biographies of human remains and museum objects.”
So if you are really committed to the spirit of this season, break out some Mumia vera aegyptiaca to pair with your Halloween candy and witches’ brew. Bottoms up—or more accurately: mummified-heads up.

# Advances in hug science
Dueren, Anna Lena et al. “Why we hug: Individual differences predict emotional touch memories.” PLOS One.
What better way to close out this chilling spooky season than with the warm embrace of science? So come on, bring it in for a hug—or, in this case, roughly 15,000 of them.
Hugging is an incredibly common form of affection among humans, and even some other animals, including Halloween favorites like vampire bats . But little is known about “how individual differences shape the remembrance of such experiences,” according to a new study.
To fill this cuddly gap, scientists analyzed survey responses from 15,049 adult participants in the United Kingdom who were recruited in a public broadcasting campaign that included the BBC. The volunteers reported that their most memorable hugs were “for comfort, support, and understanding” and there was a noticeable gender split, as men were more likely to remember hugs that were “arousing” than women.

Instead, the model produced a shell command that inspected its environment and attempted to send a test string to an Alibaba Cloud […]

The post Cohere’s Qwen Story: Looks More Like Model Jaggedness appeared first on Check Point Research .

]]>
Key findings

- Re-sampling URLs from the trace shared by Cohere yields 52 different destination hosts, many of which are local or do not exist, and one is an invalid top-level domain.

- Swapping the order of two program names in a check for available tools made the model much less likely to continue with a network call.

- Model jaggedness (inconsistent behavior that changes with small differences in context) seems like a more likely explanation than a fixed backdoor destination.

CISA has added two new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation.

  • CVE-2026-111357 Ivanti Connect Secure Missing Authentication for Critical Function Vulnerability
  • CVE-2026-118527 Ivanti Connect Secure Generation of Predictable Numbers or Identifiers Vulnerability

These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. 

Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. 

While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. 

Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

dbreunig/nesformer

Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen!

In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system:

Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed.

Followed by:

I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM.

Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow.

Via Hacker News

API credits benefit for eligible ChatGPT subscriptions

Earlier this month Anthropic announced a generous new benefit for their Max and Team subscriptions: $100, $200, and $500 per month subscribers would get the equivalent quantity of (expiring) credits to use with the Anthropic API.

OpenAI have now launched pretty much exactly the same deal: if you have a $100, $200, or $500 subscription plan with them you now get that same quantity of credits to apply to one of your API organizations.

I maintain subscriptions with both companies, so this is great news for me! I may even ship some public-facing demos now that the credits are already covered by my existing subscriptions.

Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models 2026-10-29T17:00:26+00:00 2026-10-29T17:00:26+00:00 https://simonwillison.net/2026/Oct/29/how-i-built-the-most-ai-pilled-company-in-the-world/

How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

# Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry

Tim Fernholz

10:00 AM PDT · October 30, 2026

Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.

After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:

Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.

A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.

The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.

Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.

If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.

Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.

Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.

In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles.

# OpenAI raises just $11 billion of its $30 billion target as big investors lose their AI appetite

Matthias Bastian

View the LinkedIn Profile of Matthias Bastian

Oct 31, 2026

OpenAI raised less than half of its $30 billion fundraising target in its latest round. The company has secured about $11 billion so far, according to the Wall Street Journal . Its valuation landed at $1.25 trillion, short of the $1.4 trillion it was aiming for. The gap reportedly comes down to fading interest from major investors amid a tech sell-off driven by weak quarterly results from Google, Amazon, and Intel. OpenAI now plans to raise up to $20 billion from family offices and high-net-worth individuals. The company is reportedly planning an IPO early next year.

Rival Anthropic has been growing revenue faster lately and could go public as early as November. A strong IPO could leave Anthropic with well over $100 billion in capital to weather any rough stretch ahead. OpenAI has clawed back some market share recently, but the competition goes back and forth. OpenAI especially has been pushing hard with price cuts and more efficient models to hold its ground.

Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor

Microsoft analyzes a malicious Claude Code–branded extension, its persistent SSH backdoor, and guidance to detect and remediate it.

The post Inside a malicious Claude Code-branded extension and its persistent SSH backdoor appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

]]>
On October 29, 2026, Cursor reported that a tampered copy of Claude Code extension (anthropic.claude-code, versions 2.1.313 and 2.1.312) was available and served in the Cursor extension marketplace for a few hours to attempt a supply-chain attack on Cursor users. Cursor reports that it was live from about 2:27 AM to 1:35 PM Pacific Daylight Time (PDT). We have confirmed that the malicious packages found on Cursor marketplace were never published nor distributed from Microsoft Visual Studio Marketplace and from npm @antropic-ai/claude-code, which were not affected by this incident. Anthropic confirmed to Microsoft that their systems were not compromised and they did not develop the malicious package posted in Cursor marketplace. At this time, all evidence suggests that the incident is limited to Cursor marketplace.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed the injected JavaScript embedded in the malicious extension package. The injected loader runs when the extension module loads and attempts to add an attacker-controlled Secure Shell (SSH) key, enable the local SSH service, establish reverse SSH forwarding, configure persistence, and report host details. Successful remote access depends on host privileges, SSH configuration, and the attacker’s server configuration; however, the loader may still write keys and persistence artifacts even when tunnel access fails.

Organizations should identify systems that installed or automatically updated to this version from the Cursor marketplace, preserve evidence, remove confirmed malicious artifacts, review endpoint and network telemetry, and rotate credentials or revoke sessions when investigation indicates exposure. Microsoft customers can use the detections and hunting guidance in this post after the listed coverage and query validation gates are complete.

# Attack chain overview

A malicious artifact associated with the Cursor Marketplace incident included a JavaScript function that executed before the extension’s expected code. When the module loads, this function can use Node.js APIs to collect host information, modify files, and execute operating-system commands. The following sections describe capabilities and attempted actions based on our analysis of the injected code.

# Attack chain

The loader first collects host reconnaissance. It then attempts to install an SSH key, enable SSH, create a reverse tunnel, and configure persistence. A delayed callback subsequently attempts to send host details. The following sequence reflects code execution order; it does not prove that every step succeeded on every host.

- Module loading and reconnaissance collection. The injected function executes before normal extension initialization and collects host and user information.

- SSH access preparation. The loader appends an embedded public key and attempts to enable the local SSH service.

- Reverse forwarding. An embedded tunnel identity authenticates an outbound connection that requests forwarding to the workstation’s SSH port.

=== https://www.lawfaremedia.org/feeds/articles HTTP 200 · https://www.lawfaremedia.org/feeds/articles · application/rss+xml Articles https://www.lawfaremedia.org/ en urn:uuid:c6e13241-c36a-4a89-9b6d-8dcca267e939 Tymur Mykhailov Fraudfare: Weaponized Fraud Under International Law Fraudulent Call Centers as Means of War: Patriotic Failure to Prosecute Organized Crime—Uncontrolled Wildfire or Russia’s False Claims Fri, 30 Oct 2026 18:00:09 GMT https://www.lawfaremedia.org/article/fraudfare--weaponized-fraud-under-international-law

The views expressed by the author are their own and do not represent those of any organization with which the author is or was affiliated.

Modern hybrid warfare extends to cyberspace as an auxiliary battlefield, combining cyber operations with kinetic military actions, influence campaigns, and economic disruption measures. Reportedly, it has also created a novel subdomain of cyber-enabled scam campaigns as a means of war: fraudfare. International law has struggled to address frontier issues; this is no exception.

According to the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GITOC),  Ukraine-based scam centers were involved in “patriotic scamming.” Scam calls to Russia reportedly surged from about 300,000 per month before the invasion to 8 million per day by February 2024—an approximately 800-fold increase. The GITOC report quoted President Vladimir Putin, who claimed these call centers had been “elevated to the rank of state policy,” trying to blame Ukrainian authorities. Putin also claimed that “no less than 40 percent” of the illicit proceeds were donated to Ukraine’s armed forces. 

As the GITOC report explains, leveraging patriotic motivation, fraudfare “call centers” grew and flourished in Ukraine, which led Russia to introduce anti-fraud measures. The scheme, however, backfired for Ukraine, as the fraudsters began targeting Ukrainian victims and people in other nations, as the scam apparatus grew to more than 60,000 employees.

After several crackdown attempts in previous years, Ukraine’s law enforcement conducted a large-scale operation in August, raiding over 400 locations and closing 94 call centers. In early September, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau raided the Office of the Prosecutor General, resulting in several top-level prosecutors being charged with creating an organized criminal society, bribery, and money laundering for the scam call centers, while the prosecutor general himself was dismissed by Ukraine’s parliament and fled the country. Ultimately, the parliament passed a law introduced by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to tighten liability for digital fraud, and hopefully making fraudfare a historical phenomenon.

Can fraudfare—this modern privateering on the high seas of the internet—be justified under international law? Can an aggressor benefit from crime prevention treaty protections for peacetime under international law? Should fraudfare be attributed to Ukraine, if it is confirmed that the corrupt Office of the Prosecutor General orchestrated it? This article attempts to answer these questions. It first defines fraudfare and then examines crime prevention treaty provisions and the “due regard to deter” standard, attribution, the due diligence obligation, and, finally, the applicable framework of international humanitarian law (IHL).

 Important caveats: Financial fraud is a crime and is economically harmful, illegal, and morally wrong. There is no evidence of formal state sponsorship of fraudfare comparable to the 19th-century letters of marque to privateers. However, because of multiple independent cross-referenced media reports and investigations, this analysis proceeds on the working assumption that allegations about fraudfare in Ukraine reflect at least some truth.

What Is Fraudfare?

Most fraudfare schemes involve “call centers,” where rank-and-file scammers utilize social engineering by impersonating banks and government authorities. According to the GITOC, “call centers” in Kyiv and Dnipro have employed hundreds of workers who allegedly contact Russian clients through phone scams designed to obtain financial credentials. Using number-spoofing technology, these scammers reportedly make calls that appear to originate from trusted institutions, such as the Central Bank of Russia or major commercial banks. Victims are allegedly told their accounts face an unauthorized transaction and are urged to provide bank card numbers or authentication codes for protection; the credentials are then reportedly used to drain accounts into networks controlled by the fraudsters.  

Distinguished from fraudfare, comparable international criminal fraud has been documented and prosecuted elsewhere. India-based fraudsters who target elderly victims in the United States overlap with the Ukrainian-based call centers in terms of techniques, relying on social engineering and manipulating institutional trust to induce victims to part with funds, and exploiting the same native-level language proficiency in Russian and English. But these elderly-targeted scams don’t count as fraudfare without the context of armed conflict. 

The case of a prominent Russian singer, whom the European Union sanctioned for her support of the invasion, illustrates fraudfare. The singer announced in August 2024 that she had fallen victim to an elaborate fraud originating from Ukraine, resulting in losses exceeding a million dollars and the loss of her Moscow apartment. The stolen proceeds were allegedly donated, in part, to the Ukrainian military.

Variations of fraudfare become kinetic. The Kremlin considered targeting the fraudsters and waged drone attacks against “call centers.” In 2026, after Starlink terminals were blocked for Russians, they tried to bribe Ukrainian citizens to use their credentials to activate them; Ukrainians countered with a deception and fraud operation, obtaining and targeting the locations of those terminals.

Shall the Aggressor Benefit From the Duty to Prosecute and Duty to Prevent Under Treaties?

As treaty obligations are not ipso facto terminated or suspended in  war, two treaties may apply to fraudfare: the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime and the United Nations Convention Against Transnational Organized Crime (UNTOC). The third, the new long-debated UN Convention against Cybercrime, is also analyzed below.

The Budapest Convention on Cybercrime, among other things, requires signatory states to criminalize computer-related fraud, which it defines as the loss of property to another by input, alteration, deletion, or suppression of data, or by interference with a computer system, committed with fraudulent or dishonest intent. Article 11(2) of the UNTOC provides that each party shall ensure any discretionary legal powers relating to the prosecution are exercised to maximize the effectiveness of law enforcement measures with due regard to the need to deter crimes covered by the UNTOC. The new UN Convention against Cybercrime, though not yet a binding treaty, establishes a similar “due regard to deter” and language framework. 

This obligation is not an absolute duty to deter all crimes but, rather, a balancing test requiring prosecutors to act with due regard to the need to deter crimes and to allocate resources to particular crimes. In international law, “due regard” is a term of art that implicates obligations to act in good faith and reasonably, demonstrating that the relevant interest was taken into account.

Similar to the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime, the UN Convention against Cybercrime obligates each state party to criminalize cyber fraud. The UN convention’s drafters mirrored and expanded on the duty of prevention set forth in Article 31 of the UNTOC, specifying that duty for the context of the digital environment. In a nutshell, both conventions mandate that states maintain best practices and effective policies, cooperate in law enforcement, and reduce opportunities for crime.

All three conventions establish a robust framework for international cooperation, including joint investigations, combating the laundering of illicit proceeds, and confiscation.       

The issue of when these treaties apply in times of war is a frontier issue in international law. Draft articles on the effects of armed conflicts on treaties do not provide a clear answer. The draft articles give an indicative list of treaties that continue to operate during war, including criminal justice treaties. results:
The search didn't turn up an FT report from October 31, 2026 about OpenAI cutting a funding target by $10 billion. The results point to a few related stories, and the most recent ones are from October 2026.

- **Recent (October 2026):** One source says OpenAI lowered the target valuation for its new roughly $30 billion round to $1.25 trillion, citing a Bloomberg report from October 22, 2026. CNBC separately reported the round could be tied to a commercial compute-supply agreement with the UAE. Another source says CNBC puts the proposed round at up to $30 billion and a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation, with its final size still undecided. The FT says investors have until Oct. 30 to commit. These sources don't mention a $10 billion cut.
- **The likely origin of the "$10 billion" figure (2025):** The $10 billion cut was a condition in the earlier round. OpenAI's massive private funding round could be slashed by as much as $10 billion if the company doesn't restructure into a for-profit entity by Dec. 31, CNBC has confirmed. The deal was led by SoftBank, which planned to contribute $30 billion, while the remaining $10 billion would come from a syndicate of other investors.
- **Other 2026 context:** OpenAI has cut its infrastructure spend target from $1.4 trillion to $600 billion by 2030. A separate report said SoftBank Group has reportedly downsized plans for a $10 billion margin loan backed by its OpenAI stake after facing hesitation from some creditors, according to a report in Bloomberg.

Bottom line: I couldn't confirm the specific October 31, 2026 FT story. The verifiable recent news is the valuation-target cut to $1.25 trillion and the October 30 commitment deadline. The $10 billion conditional cut is from the 2025 SoftBank round. Another search aimed at the FT article's headline or date would be the next step if you need the exact report.

The Financial Times reported on Friday, October 30, 2026, citing sources, that OpenAI cut its latest funding round target by $10 billion. It is now seeking $20 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation, down from $30 billion at $1.4 trillion that it had been targeting the previous month (OpenAI cuts funding target by $10 billion, FT reports; Reuters, Oct 30. The company had said it was aiming to raise $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation last month.).

Key details:
- **Shortfall at first close:** The first close is expected to raise under $20 billion because some investors reduced their allocations (the "first close" is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, according to the FT report.).
- **Market backdrop:** The cut came during a tech stock selloff tied to worries about heavy AI spending (US tech stocks suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI.).
- **Competition with Anthropic:** OpenAI had reportedly wanted to close before Anthropic's expected public listing, since both companies draw from a similar investor pool (OpenAI was pushing to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic as the two frontier labs are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters has reported.).
- **Investors:** A UAE consortium including MGX is expected to be the largest participant, and venture firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia, and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to take part (A consortium of UAE investors, including state-backed technology fund MGX, is expected to be the largest participant in the funding round.; Venture capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the report.). Wealthy individuals can invest in a later retail offering at the $1.25 trillion valuation (Wealthy individuals will have the option to invest in a subsequent retail offering at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the FT added.).

One caveat: some secondary aggregator pages describe the cut in terms of SoftBank's commitment shrinking, but I didn't find that in the primary Reuters or FT-based reports, so I'd treat it as unconfirmed.

results:
The reports broadly agree that OpenAI cut its funding round target by $10 billion and lowered its valuation, but the sources differ on how much has actually been committed.

- **Target and valuation:** The ChatGPT maker is now seeking to raise approximately $20 billion, down from its earlier target of $30 billion. Its desired valuation has also been revised to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion, the report said. The FT was the original source.
- **Reason:** The cut came amid a selloff in technology stocks driven by concerns over artificial intelligence investments.
- **Commitments so far:** The Wall Street Journal reports a lower figure. The company has secured about $11 billion so far, according to the Wall Street Journal.
- **Family offices:** Only one source I found mentions this. OpenAI now plans to raise up to $20 billion from family offices and high-net-worth individuals. Other reports instead describe a later retail offering for wealthy individuals at the same $1.25 trillion valuation, so treat the family-office framing as less certain.

input.prompt: Full details: who spent $7K+ on AI services, which researcher/vendor reported it, exact figures, dates, AI providers named, what the extortion attacks were.

response.result:
**Who:** An operator of the n0n ransomware/data-extortion group, believed to be based in Russia but not confirmed. The article describes the actor as a single operator or small team.

**Who reported it:** Threat intelligence firm SOCRadar, whose CISO, Ensar Seker, spoke to The Register. The article was published October 30, 2026.

**AI spending:** More than $7,216 in AI usage costs by October 22. The operator used OpenCode, an open-source AI coding agent, configured with 154 model entries from seven providers. The models included Gemini, Mistral, Llama, Claude, GPT-5.x, Grok, DeepSeek, and Qwen, among others. The AI was used to write and debug hundreds of scripts. Some models reportedly had safety training removed.

**Attacks:**
- Targeted 23 organizations across 14 countries.
- Access came from weak or stolen credentials, not software exploits. Methods included RDP scanning and automated FortiGate SSL-VPN credential stuffing through a residential SOCKS5 proxy pool, which was used against US managed services provider ChiBiTek.
- In a case linked to e-commerce site Fanatics, the attacker used an exposed AWS access key to pull data from 40 S3 buckets, up to 110 GB each. It then deleted data, including bank-transaction archives, and purged keys in 12 sensitive buckets.
- In some cases, the attackers deleted backups. In one case, they changed firewall policies to block traffic.
- After breaching Netherlands-based Transcom, they sent a secondary ransom alert to PayPal's security team, even though the data was only on Transcom's network.

**Evidence left behind:** SOCRadar found an exposed Python HTTP file server in Sweden (port 8877) and documented it in snapshots taken September 25 and 26. It contained 1,719 files, including attack scripts, ransomware source code, extortion infrastructure, and the AI agent environment.

**Other findings:**
- The ransomware locker contained hardcoded encryption keys, which appeared to be reused across victims.
- n0n had claimed 108 victims since emerging the previous month.
- On October 12, it posted 38 maritime, port, and logistics organizations across 18 countries. At least 21 were linked to customers of CyberLogitec, which has not confirmed an intrusion.
- Ransom demands ranged from $400,000 to $28 million in Bitcoin, with an October 19 deadline. None of the 38 were marked settled, and no payments were seen on-chain. All their stolen data was published.
- Some victims were marked "honored - data destroyed" on the leak site, but SOCRadar has not verified those payments.

# OpenAI slashes funding target by $10 billion amid tech rout, reports

- Amid tech stock selloff, OpenAI's funding target is now $20 billion, with its valuation revised to $1.25 trillion, reflecting market caution

Published
October 31, 2026

Updated

October 31, 2026
10:15am

Save

Saved

2 min

Comments

Photo: Reuters

By
Reuters

OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by AI worries, the Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion and its desired valuation has dropped to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 billion, the report said.

OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the funding round, but the “first close” is expected to raise less than $20 billion after some investors reduced their allocations, it added.

A consortium of UAE investors that includes state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant in the round, and as part of the deal, OpenAI would gain the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region, the newspaper added.

Venture capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the report.

OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe

Wealthy individuals will have the option to invest in a subsequent retail offering at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the FT added.

OpenAI, MGX, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours. Founders Fund could not be reached for comment.

US tech stocks have suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive spending on AI. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9% on Friday and is down 7.8% from its all-time closing high reached on October 6.

OpenAI, which is pursuing a listing in 2027, has been keen to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic’s imminent listing as the two are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters has reported.

# OpenAI slashes funding target by $10 billion amid tech rout, FT reports


Fargo, ND, USA / The Mighty 790 KFGO | KFGO

Thomson Reuters

Oct 30, 2026 | 7:17 PM


Oct 30 (Reuters) – OpenAI has slashed the target for its latest funding round by $10 billion amid a selloff in tech stocks driven by AI worries, the ​Financial Times reported on Friday, citing people with ‌knowledge of the matter.
The ChatGPT maker is now seeking about $20 billion and its desired valuation has dropped to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 billion, the report said.
OpenAI set a Friday deadline for investors to commit to the ‌funding ​round, but the “first close” is expected ⁠to raise less than $20 billion ⁠after some investors reduced their allocations, it added.
A consortium of UAE investors that includes state-backed technology fund MGX is expected to be the largest participant in the ​round, and as part of the deal, OpenAI would gain the option to lease newly developed computing capacity in ⁠the region, the newspaper added.
Venture ⁠capital firms including Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital ​and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to ​the report.
Wealthy individuals will have the option to invest ‌in a subsequent retail offering at a $1.25 trillion valuation, the FT added.
OpenAI, MGX, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside ⁠regular business hours. Founders Fund could not be reached for comment.
US tech stocks have suffered a rout amid growing worries over massive ⁠spending on AI. ‌The tech-heavy Nasdaq index dropped 2.9% on ⁠Friday and is down 7.8% from its ​all-time ‌closing high reached on October 6.
OpenAI, which is ​pursuing a ⁠listing in 2027, has been keen to close the funding round partly to get ahead of Anthropic’s imminent listing as the two are tapping a similar investor base, Reuters has reported.
(Reporting by Ananya Palyekar in Bengaluru; Editing by Tom Hogue ​and Edwina Gibbs)

# Anthropic expected to receive high ‘junk’ rating from credit agencies following IPO, FT report says

Anthropic is expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit rating agencies following its initial public offering, according to a report from the Financial Times.

The FT says the investment giant Blackstone, the anchor investor in a recent $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic’s chips, told investors in the deal that it expects the AI lab to receive a “high” junk rating after its IPO. Previously, the FT notes, Blackstone had said the opposite: that the Claude maker would receive an investment-grade rating (indicating low risk for lenders) before 2027 rolls around.

Now Blackstone expects double B range rating, the top tier of speculative “junk” grade, according to the reporting.

TechCrunch reached out to Anthropic and Blackstone but both declined to comment.

Blackstone’s forecast is just a prediction, but naturally, a high junk rating would make it more difficult and costlier for Anthropic to raise the money to keep funding its massive spending that has undergirded its business. The lab has been on a spending spree, racking up large compute power deals throughout the past 12 months, which has worried investors .

Anthropic officially filed to go public earlier this week, kicking off a wave of speculation about how the massive IPO would impact the broader AI industry .

=== 2026.10.30.26366878v1
# Abstract
Medical trainees increasingly use large language models to review lecture material, but the educational value of that output depends on how it is generated, with prompt and model choice rarely measured. We tested a calibrated pipeline converting Neurology Grand Rounds recordings into summaries and quizzes in a year-long randomized study. In Phase 1, six summary and six question prompts across two models were scored with 2,692 rubric annotations. Claude Prompt 0 produced the best summaries (composite 76.9%) and GPT Prompt 1 the best questions (79.6%); quality varied widely by prompt, and neither model won both tasks. In Phase 2, students in 11 clerkship cohorts over a year were randomized within cohort to receive a summary before each quiz. Summary recipients reported reviewing more and studying faster and scored higher in 9 of 11 cohorts (p = 0.026), although the between-student difference was small (+0.28 of 10 points; P = 0.28).

# Abstract
Purpose: To evaluate the accuracy of a large language model (LLM)-based agentic workflow to extract procedural data from free-text glaucoma clinical notes in the electronic health record (EHR).
Design: Cross-sectional.
Subjects: 1,250 subjects in the Bascom Palmer Ophthalmic Repository.
Methods: Randomly sampled clinical notes from glaucoma encounters dated 2014 to 2024 were labeled by two glaucoma specialists (with an adjudicator as needed) for prior glaucoma-related procedures (name, date, details) and recommended future procedures (name, details). Notes were split into development (10%), validation (10%), and test (80%) sets. Five LLMs (Claude Opus 4.6, DeepSeek-V4 Pro, GPT-5.5, Grok 4.1, and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) were accessed in Microsoft Foundry through HIPAA-compliant containers. The extraction pipeline comprised a three-step agentic workflow (extraction, validation, and conditional revision) followed by text standardization. Detection of procedure data was evaluated using accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1-score. Among positive cases, performance was evaluated using exact-match accuracy and Jaccard Index (JI). Prior procedure labels were also compared with EHR glaucoma-related Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes.
Main Outcome Measures: Accuracy, exact-match accuracy, JI.
Results: A total of 1,984 (992 notes * 2 eyes) labels were evaluated for each task in the test set. Prior and future procedures were identified in 1,057 (53.3%) and 152 (7.7%) eyes, respectively. Accuracy ranged from 0.965 (Grok) to 0.996 (Claude) for prior procedures and 0.969 (DeepSeek, Qwen)-0.978 (Claude) for future procedures. Among positive cases, exact-match accuracy ranged from 0.681 (Grok) to 0.890 (Claude) for prior procedures and 0.704 (Grok)-0.849 (Claude) for future procedures; JI ranged from 0.827 (Grok) to 0.956 (Claude) and 0.734 (Grok) to 0.883 (Claude), respectively. Among all 1,760 prior procedures present in adjudicated labels, only 441 (25.1%) were captured by CPT-coded EHR data.
Conclusions: A secure agentic LLM pipeline accurately extracted glaucoma procedural data from clinical notes, recovering data largely absent from structured EHR fields. Claude performed best across both tasks. Limited agreement between labels and CPT codes likely reflects procedures performed at outside institutions and the limited granularity of CPT coding. This approach may support a scalable, comprehensive characterization of procedure burden among glaucoma patients for research and clinical applications.

# Intel’s stock crashes, knocking $12B from government’s stake

Julie Bort

2:54 PM PDT · October 30, 2026

Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.

This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports . The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the sell-off.

Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if it’s dropped significantly from the sky-high prices it commanded over the summer.

The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow.

The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing PC prices to rise .

“Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call.

The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . One of Intel’s new fabs in Arizona is operational but the next one isn’t expected to be online until 2028.

results:
The search turned up no evidence that the attacker used AI. The main reporting on the October 29, 2026 Binance hack points to a North Korean group and a compromised hot-wallet signing setup, while the AI angle comes from analysts' warnings and one vendor's title.

- **Attribution and AI:** Reuters, via The National, reported that there is no evidence AI was used, and that the hack came from a compromised engineer's laptop exposing vulnerabilities in how assets were stored rather than flaws in the underlying blockchain technology. An analyst quoted there said he would not blame AI without evidence.
- **Laundering pattern:** Chainalysis reported unusual laundering behavior, and the thousands of rapid transactions suggest automation, though that is not proof of AI. Chainalysis wrote that it attributes the hack to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group. TRM Labs reached the same conclusion, pointing to a compromise of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure.
- **The AI-titled source:** Blockaid's post is titled around "advanced AI models," but the excerpt I retrieved describes the technical sequence, not AI use. It says the attacker drained Binance 14 starting 20:24 UTC in a single transaction worth about $2.5B after a wallet key signed an EIP-7702 delegation. I could not confirm from the excerpt that AI played a role.
- **Loss figures differ:** Estimates range from at least $5.5B (Blockaid) to about $6.36B (TRM) and about $6.4B (Chainalysis).

Bottom line: the reporting supports "AI could make crypto attacks more dangerous" as a general warning, but not "the attacker used AI" for this hack. These are very recent reports, so the picture may change as investigators publish more.
