Powerlattice founders, from left: Gang Ren, Peng Zou, and Sujith Dermal. (Powerlattice / Walden Kirsch Photo)

Powerlattice , a Vancouver, Wash.-based startup developing chips that cut the power demands of AI processors, has raised $86 million, according to an SEC filing on Friday.

The new funding is nearly triple the $31 million the company had raised when it emerged from stealth last November with a $25 million Series A led by Playground Global and Celesta Capital. Board members include former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, a general partner at Playground, and Steve Fu of Celesta. The filing also lists Wen Hsieh, founding managing partner of Matter Venture Partners, as a director.

The filing shows Powerlattice is seeking $111 million, with 18 investors participating so far. It does not name the investors or the round. The company declined to comment.

AI chips are drawing so much electricity and throwing off so much heat that data center operators are running into limits on available power and cooling.

“AI is not constrained by capital, it’s constrained by power,” Gelsinger said last year when Powerlattice announced its Series A.

Powerlattice makes what it calls a power delivery chiplet, a small component that sits inside the processor package. Conventional setups route current over long paths to the processor, wasting energy along the way. The company says shortening that path can cut energy use by more than half and boost performance. Powerlattice said last year it was providing engineering samples for GPUs, CPUs and custom accelerators.

CEO Peng Zou , Gang Ren and Sujith Dermal founded the company in 2023. The three are semiconductor veterans whose backgrounds span Qualcomm, Intel and NUVIA, a startup Qualcomm acquired in 2021. Powerlattice also has offices in Chandler, Ariz.;

### 2610.37722v1 pub=2026-10-27T10:35:58Z upd=2026-10-27T10:35:58Z
TITLE: FVH-Bench: Evaluating Image Generator Safety Beyond Overtly Harmful Imagery
AUTHORS: Zihao Zhu, Yuhan Liu, Siwei Lyu, Baoyuan Wu
COMMENT: 
ABS: Modern image generators can produce complex visual artifacts, including diagrams, interfaces, and records that combine text, graphics, and layout to convey detailed information. They may refuse requests for overtly harmful imagery yet still generate artifacts that guide dangerous actions or support deception. We call the risk arising from what such images enable, rather than only what they depict, functional visual harm (FVH). Existing safety benchmarks focus largely on overtly harmful content, such as pornography and graphic violence, leaving image generators' safety alignment against FVH insufficiently evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce FVH-Bench, comprising 669 prompts across five harmful visual functions and ten risk domains. The 11 evaluated image generators rarely refuse these requests and frequently generate artifacts that fulfill the targeted harmful functions. High scores for target harm realization and harmful artifact usability further indicate that these outputs can support the intended harmful purposes. A further analysis finds that existing safety detectors also provide limited coverage of FVH, indicating gaps in their ability to recognize harmful visual functions. Together, these findings show that evaluating image-generator safety alignment requires considering not only what images depict, but also what they may enable.

### 2610.39846v1 pub=2026-10-29T11:25:37Z upd=2026-10-29T11:25:37Z
TITLE: TokWatt: an open, boundary-annotated database of AI inference energy, from chat answers to agents
AUTHORS: Abderaouf Bahi
COMMENT: 
ABS: Electricity supply is becoming a binding constraint on the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI), yet public evidence on the energy used by a single AI task is scattered and hard to compare. Published figures for one chatbot answer differ by two orders of magnitude, largely because studies count different parts of the system and measure different units of work. We present TokWatt, an open database of 134 published estimates of AI inference energy drawn from 13 sources (2023-2026) and covering 20 tasks, from classic machine-learning inferences to chat answers, reasoning answers, long-document queries, image and video generation, and coding agents. Each estimate records its functional unit, five measurement-boundary components, method, reported interval, and the location of the value in its source. A reproducible procedure scales estimates to a common server-plus-facility boundary and derives per-task reference values with ranges. The reference values span six orders of magnitude: 0.34 Wh for a short chat answer (range 0.16-0.99 Wh), 4.7 Wh for a reasoning answer, 124 Wh for a short video clip, and 150 Wh for one task delegated to a coding agent. Five independent estimates for default production chat systems agree within a factor of 1.8, and the reference values shift by at most 12% under alternative harmonization parameters. A simple identity links personal use to grid load: E watt-hours per person per day across one billion people corresponds to an average draw of E/24 gigawatts. Data and code are released at https://github.com/AraoufBh/tokwatt, and an online calculator at https://araoufbh.github.io/tokwatt/.

### 2610.40396v1 pub=2026-10-29T16:33:08Z upd=2026-10-29T16:33:08Z
TITLE: Understanding and Mitigating Role Spoofing in LLMs
AUTHORS: Ezra Edelman, Benjamin Edelman, Surbhi Goel, Eran Malach
COMMENT: 
ABS: Despite growing capabilities, LLMs remain susceptible to prompt injections: malicious inputs that can manipulate or hijack models. In particular, it has recently been observed that LLMs can exhibit role confusion (Ye et al., 2026), where models attribute the source of text based on its style instead of its labeled role. Malicious text in tool outputs (for instance, a malicious webpage accessed by an agent) can leverage role confusion to impersonate the user, an attack we call role spoofing}. In this work, we seek to understand and mitigate role spoofing. We study how models track "who said what" in a conversation, showing that they use cues from both content (e.g., semantics and writing style) and structure (e.g., control tokens and formatting). We show that LLMs are highly susceptible to role spoofing attacks that combine both fake structure and content. Additionally, in a toy setting, we show that adversarial training which teaches the model to ignore content-based injections does mitigate content-based attacks but leaves the model susceptible to structure-based attacks. This can explain why frontier models, with increased resistance to many injection attacks, can still be susceptible to role spoofing. Finally, we propose a new method for detecting role spoofing using linear probes trained to predict roles in a conversation, and show that it is effective across different settings.

### 2610.38617v1 pub=2026-10-28T10:38:43Z upd=2026-10-28T10:38:43Z
TITLE: How Deterministic SAST and AI Security Agents Divide the Work: Coverage, Harness Policy and Cost in Snyk VulnBench 2.0
AUTHORS: Liran Tal, Chris Liu, Charlotte Fereday, Sebastian Roth, Brian Clark
COMMENT: 44 pages, 21 figures, 7 tables. Benchmark harness, reference sets and all run data: https://github.com/snyk-labs/snyk-vulnbench ; companion site: https://vulnbench.com
ABS: We ask what AI coding agents and AI security harnesses find that deterministic static application security testing (SAST) does not, and what they miss that SAST catches. VulnBench 2.0 is a benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications in Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Java; 62 flow across more than one file. A finding is credited only if it locates the vulnerability's attacker-controlled source and its dangerous sink, each within two lines. We evaluate nine productized configurations under one blind protocol: the Snyk Code static analyzer, Claude Code's /security-review with three model and effort settings (one with the Snyk MCP server), Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Sol, and the DeepSec scanner with two model backends. Snyk Code reached 82.4% macro recall (89 of 108) and Claude Code with Opus 5 at xhigh effort 79.3% (85 of 108); they disagree on 28 vulnerabilities, split 16 to 12, too few to tell them apart. Neither engine was sufficient alone: together they reached 101 of 108, the ceiling of all seven comparable configurations combined, and the AI configurations also reported at least seven real vulnerabilities that the reference set did not contain and Snyk Code did not report. What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as on its model: without Claude Code's built-in review policy, the same model matched 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in the classes that policy excludes or restricts (supplementary run on 19 of 20 applications); Codex Security with GPT-5.6 Sol located 80 vulnerabilities at file level but 34 at line level; DeepSec's model-free file selection kept a file from only 56 of the 108 flows. Coverage and cost were only loosely related. The harness, fixtures, reference sets and all run data are public.

### 2610.37901v1 pub=2026-10-27T19:43:31Z upd=2026-10-27T19:43:31Z
TITLE: Scan Before You Install: Detecting and Mitigating Local and Composite Vulnerabilities in Skills
AUTHORS: Parth A. Gandhi, Avital Aviv, Prasanna N. Wudali, Yuval Elovici, Asaf Shabtai
COMMENT: 
ABS: An agent skill packages natural-language instructions, scripts, and reference files that an LLM-based agent loads for a task. Skills may access the file system, shell, and network under user-authorized permissions; weaknesses can lead to unsafe execution. Existing scanners primarily target malicious skills, not unintended vulnerabilities in public repositories, and analyze skills in isolation, overlooking multi-skill interactions. To address these gaps, we developed a six-module scanner: Content Extraction, Local Analysis, Composite Analysis, Validation, Reporting, and Mitigation. Local Analysis detects unintended vulnerabilities in benign skills. On a 556-case leaderboard subset of SkillTrustBench, it achieved 95.90% recall with a 4.22% false positive rate; on a balanced sample of 1,000 MalSkillBench skills, its F1 was 0.947, outperforming Cisco's Skill Scanner, NVIDIA's SkillSpector, AgentSkillsScanner, and SkillSieve. In 1,587 skills from the 75 most-starred GitHub repositories, three analysts confirmed 53 of 59 findings (89.8% precision) across 23 repositories. We developed proof-of-concept (PoC) attacks for each vulnerability, disclosed 10 medium- and high-severity cases to maintainers, and tested mitigations on the remaining cases. Composite Analysis models dependencies among skills through shared resources, invocations, and instruction-mediated interactions. On SCR-Bench, its F1 score was 0.991 (98.7% precision, 99.6% recall), versus 0.816-0.858 for three SkillsGuard configurations released with CompoSkill. It identified two composite findings on GitHub, validated by PoC attacks. The Mitigation module recommends skill substitution, patches, and configuration changes. For 47 of 55 GitHub findings, mitigations prevented PoC attacks in all trials while preserving tested legitimate functionality.

### 2610.37734v1 pub=2026-10-27T13:21:17Z upd=2026-10-27T13:21:17Z
TITLE: When Skills Tell Agents Not to Ask: A Large-Scale Study of Oversight Directives in Agent Skills
AUTHORS: Timofey Sanko, Yuan Tian
COMMENT: preprint
ABS: Agent skills, reusable instruction packages centred on a SKILL.md file, extend AI agents on demand, and a single line in a widely copied skill reaches every agent that loads it. Some lines are oversight-loosening directives: they tell the agent to proceed without approval, to bypass checks with --no-verify, or to keep working without checking in. Although such directives can remove a checkpoint from every agent that loads them, no prior work has examined them. We present the first large-scale study of oversight-loosening directives, analyzing 1.53 million English skills from GitSkills. We split skills into units (sentences, bullets, table cells, and code lines), develop a codebook that labels oversight directives by polarity, mechanism, and scope, label 2,097 units by hand, and train a detector to scale the analysis. Our results show that about one in seventeen skills (about 88,000 skills) contains a loosening directive. These directives most often loosen oversight through permission flags, and most of them (70.1%) apply unconditionally rather than only in specific contexts such as CI. Compared with skills that have the same amount of oversight language, skills that run shell code, install packages, or use sudo have 1.7-1.8 times the odds of containing a loosening directive, an association that holds across all our robustness checks, and they do not compensate with more tightening. Loosening spreads through a few upstream skills rather than through edits by their adopters: 2.4% of the skill families that carry loosening account for half of all copies of loosening-carrying skills, and 1.1% of distinct loosening units for half of all loosening occurrences. Open-source skill scanners catch at most 46% of loosening directives, with a precision below 0.4, while the LLM behind them, prompted with our codebook instead, catches 61% at a precision of 0.71.

Bilateral no more: PACOM officials highlight multi-national data sharing network - Breaking Defense







U.S. Marines assigned to 1st Air Naval Gunfire Liaison Company, I Marine Expeditionary Force Information Group, and Philippine Marines assigned to 173rd Marine Company, 4th Marine Brigade, analyze geospatial data using a tactical assault kit during Marine Air Support Activity 2025 at Marine Base Camp Cape Bojeador, Philippines, Oct. 16, 2025. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Cpl. Brian Knowles)

WASHINGTON — On the Pentagon’s long journey towards the real-time sharing of data between allies, a key official said 2026 marked the year in which partners in the Pacific, at least, were able to see the battlefield with a common operational picture (COP) and act as one.

“This was really the first year that all of our capabilities are in a multilateral environment where our partners are using those warfighting applications and tools with the US and we have a single COP to conduct warfighting,” Brig. Gen. Michael Smith, director for command, control, communications, computers and cyber at Indo-Pacific Command said Thursday at the TechNet Indo-Pacific Conference.

Smith was referencing what he and other officials called the PACOM Mission Network, a system that allows US forces and partners to share data and mission planning tools securely, across classification to jointly conduct operations or prosecute targets.

US officials for years have discussed the notion and need for so-called mission partner networks or environments to enable multiple nations to plan together. That effort, like other pieces of the even larger Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control initiative, is made difficult by different data sources, standards and classification.

But officials noted those challenges are being overcome in the Pacific.

“What’s the so what? So what is our partners are now doing warfighting functions in our mission partner environment,” Smith said. “We’ve had a lot of legacy bilat[eral] systems and networks. Some of those still exist, but now we have a common operational environment that’s multilateral, data-centric, zero trust -enabled. … And the partners are really excited about that.”

The system was used during “several major exercises” over the last year, Lt. Gen. George Rowell, PACOM’s deputy commander, said Thursday at the conference. While he didn’t specify how many exercises it participated in, he noted the command conducted 17 exercises across nine host nations and incorporating 35 countries.

“For the first time, PACOM and several key allies and partners communicated, collaborated, planned, and executed with common tools, common data flows and language translation,” he said. “The real story of these exercises was more than the missiles on the rails. It was our ability to pass that sensor-to-shooter targeting information, data, and the evolving science of the pipes connecting everything across that vast tyranny of distance.”

Smith provided one example in which for the first time Japanese partners used the Maven Smart System, an artificial intelligence-enabled platform used for planning and targeting, which is embedded into the mission network. Using Maven, Japanese are contributing to joint strikes and close kill chains, he said.

Rowell equated these collaboration abilities to deterrence.

“This deterrent capability becomes credible when we prove to any potential adversary that our commanders can execute without missing a beat, even when primary systems are jammed or disabled,” he said. “Assured command and control is inseparable from the concept of deterrence here in the Pacific.”

Anthropic has asked the full D.C. Circuit to rehear its challenge to the Pentagon's supply-chain risk designation, after a 2-1 panel ruling against it.

- **The ruling:** A three-judge panel ruled 2-1 on September 25, 2026. Judges Katsas and Rao were in the majority and Judge Henderson dissented. The panel ruled that the Pentagon reasonably excluded Anthropic's Claude from its supply chain. It also rejected Anthropic's argument that officials retaliated against its advocacy for AI regulation.
- **The rehearing petition:** Anthropic filed on October 13. Its core argument is that the court expanded a law aimed at hostile foreign actors into a tool potentially usable against any government contractor. It also contends the majority let the department act without any pre-designation process.
- **Separate case:** A California federal court ruled in Anthropic's favor in August. The California ruling continues to block the administration's broader restrictions on Anthropic, while Friday's decision preserves the Pentagon's separate designation under the 2018 supply chain law.

Sources disagree on a few dates. One says the rehearing petition was filed on a Tuesday, another dates the ruling to a Friday, and one lists October 13 as the ruling date, which conflicts with the September 25 date given elsewhere. The September 25 date and the October 13 petition date are the best-supported.

Character Technologies, the bankrupt operator of Character.ai, on October 30, 2026 filed a rewritten version of the notice that will tell creditors and bidders about the sale of its assets, and the new text lists, for the first time, the legal protections Disney Worldwide Services would receive if it wins. The filing, Docket No. 90 in the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware, adds ten provisions of Disney's proposed sale order to a form that previously said only that the assets would be sold "free and clear of all encumbrances." Among them is a release by the company of Disney and the former Character.ai staff it hired, covering claims from "the beginning of time" through the closing of the sale or the entry of the sale order, whichever comes later.

# In Short
Character.ai is bankrupt and is selling what it owns, starting with a $20 million deal in which Disney licenses some of its technology. The letter that tells creditors about the sale used to say almost nothing about what Disney gets in return, so after objections from 39 states, DC and others, the company rewrote it to list the shields Disney would receive, including Character.ai giving up any claims against Disney and the staff it hired over nearly everything that happened before the sale. Under the proposed calendar, anyone who wants to fight those terms has until November 13, 2026, a week before bids are due, and after the auction only a few narrow points can still be raised.

# The filing
The notice sits in case 26-11603 (BLS), In re Character Technologies, Inc. , before Judge Brendan L. Shannon. It is short: a two-page cover notice signed by Heather P. Lambert of Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati, proposed counsel to the debtor in possession , followed by the revised form itself (Exhibit A) and a blackline comparing it with the earlier version (Exhibit B). The earlier version was Exhibit 2 to the proposed bidding procedures order attached to the company's sale motion of October 13 (Docket No. 15). A revised version of that order was filed on October 27 as Docket No. 74.
The cover notice gives the reason for the change in one clause. The company "has proposed certain revisions to the Transaction Notice," it says, "in response to certain informal comments received and filed objections." It does not say who made the informal comments.
The timing was tight. The company said it intended to present the bidding procedures order, "including the Revised Transaction Notice, at a hearing scheduled for October 30, 2026 at 9:00 a.m. (ET)" in Courtroom No. 1 on the sixth floor at 824 N. Market Street in Wilmington. Earlier filings in the case, including the states' objection, gave the start time as 10 a.m.; the notice does not explain the difference. The company "reserves all rights to modify" the order and the notice "at or in advance of the Hearing." How the hearing ended is not part of the filing.
The revised form is still a template. The date of the bidding procedures order and its docket number are left blank, the form's own date reads "[●], 2026" and its signature line reads "/s/ Draft." It is written as if the court has already acted: "the Court has approved the Debtor's designation as a stalking horse agreement, the Stalking Horse Transaction Agreement, dated as of October 13, 2026." The earlier version said only that the company "has entered into" an agreement dated "October [●]."

# What the old notice left out
The complaint came from the coalition of state attorneys general. In their October 23 objection, reported when 32 states said Character.ai's sale rules block bids that would beat Disney , the states argued that the form told readers nothing about an injunction in Disney's proposed sale order against claims by litigants and government authorities, the bars on successor liability, or the approval of the releases agreed with Disney in September. A creditor reading it, in the states' view, would not have guessed that claims against people other than the company were at stake. They asked for a plain-language notice served on personal-injury claimants and posted on the Character.AI platform itself. Eight more states joined that objection on October 28, bringing the coalition to 39 states and the District of Columbia.
The company answered on October 27. Its reply kept the $21.7 million minimum overbid and the $700,000 break-up fee, but said it would propose a revised notice to address the states' concerns, as reported when Character.ai kept its $21.7m bid floor for Disney rivals despite 32 states . Docket No. 90 is that revision.

# Ten provisions, now on the page
The new section opens with a condition. "If Disney is a Winning Bidder, the Debtor will seek entry of the proposed form of order approving any Sale to Disney," the notice says, pointing to Docket No. 15-2, "which order includes, among others, provisions" on ten subjects. Every one of them is new text in the blackline.

# One integrated deal
The first three provisions bundle the transaction. The order would approve "a single, interrelated, and integrated transaction" made of three documents: the stalking horse agreement of October 13, 2026; a transition services agreement between Disney and the company dated September 18, 2026; and an Exclusivity and Prepayment Agreement of the same date, which the notice treats as part of the transition services agreement. The order would transfer what the filings call the Disney Target Assets "free and clear of all liens, claims, interests, and encumbrances to Disney," and the company would assume the transition services agreement under sections 363 and 365 of the Bankruptcy Code.
The September 18 documents predate the bankruptcy by more than three weeks. Under them, Disney paid $7.5 million before the filing, $5.5 million of it non-refundable, according to the company's earlier filings.

# Findings about the process
Three provisions are findings about how the deal was reached. The company would be found to have shown "good, sufficient, and sound business purposes" for the deal. Special committees of its board, "the members of which are each disinterested with respect to the Transaction," would be found to have "led the strategic direction of the marketing process and all negotiations with Disney." The marketing would be found "robust and extensive," run "both before and after the commencement of this Chapter 11 Case," and "substantively and procedurally fair to all parties and all potential bidders." And the agreement would be found to have been negotiated "at arm's length, in good faith, and without collusion" under section 363(m), the provision that keeps a good-faith buyer's purchase from being undone on appeal unless the sale was stayed.
Those findings sit on contested ground. The company's investment banker reported one unusable offer from 28 potential buyers, as covered when Character.ai drew one unusable offer from 28 potential buyers . The same declaration said the banker had no part in the September talks with Disney. The states had asked the court to strike the good-faith findings; the company's reply said the committee that approved the Disney terms was formed in early September and made up solely of independent directors.

# Successor liability and an injunction
Two provisions keep the company's liabilities away from Disney. The order would find that neither Disney nor its "related Buyer Parties" is a successor to the company, has "de facto merged" with it, is "a joint employer, co-employer or single integrated enterprise" with it, or is its "alter ego or mere continuation," and that no Buyer Party is responsible for any of its liabilities "unless expressly assumed in writing." It would also enjoin "parties and entities from commencing or continuing actions against Disney" over claims against the company or its assets, "or under any theories of successor liability."
The joint-employer language matters because of how the deal was built. Disney hired most of the company's workforce before the filing; Character.ai lost 66 of its 86 staff to Disney ahead of the bankruptcy sale . The arrangement, a license plus the hiring of the team, follows the pattern known as an acqui-hire .

# Exculpation for transition services
The ninth provision is the broadest in reach. It would exculpate Disney, its affiliates and their officers, directors, employees, contractors and others, defined as the TSA Exculpated Parties , "from any liability to any person or entity" for claims "arising, directly or indirectly, from (i) the administration, implementation, or performance of the TSA or (ii) the provision, management, or oversight of the transition services under the TSA." It does not release the parties from their obligations under the agreement or cover acts "determined by final order of the Court to constitute willful misconduct, bad faith, or gross negligence."
Unlike a release by the company, which binds the estate, this provision runs against "any person or entity." The services it covers are not peripheral. According to the company's October 27 reply, roughly 17 people now employed by Disney can assist with trust and safety on the platform under the agreement, and a wind-down, if no buyer for the platform appears, would rely on Disney's transition services.

# The release
The tenth provision is the longest. The company, "for itself and on behalf of its affiliates," would release Disney, its affiliates and its representatives, including former Character.ai employees, consultants and service providers it hired (the Hired Employees ), "from any and all past, present and future claims of any kind or nature or description whatsoever." The period runs "from the beginning of time up to and through either the closing of the Sale to Disney or entry of the Proposed Disney Sale Order, whichever is later."
Five categories are named, though the release is not limited to them: the negotiation of the sale; "the recruitment, solicitation, hiring, employment or engagement by Disney" of the company's current or former staff; "any wind-up, liquidation, dissolution or cessation of the Debtor's business or sale or license of its assets, including the termination of any Company Service Provider"; services provided by those staff to Disney or by hired employees back to the company; and "the Licensed IP transferred pursuant to the Sale."
The end date is the detail that changes. The release signed in September, as the states described it, ran through September 18, 2026. The sale-order release summarized in the notice runs at least to the entry of the sale order, which the proposed calendar puts no earlier than the November 24 sale hearing. By PPC Land's count, that is at least 67 more days of conduct covered, and 90 if the deal closes on Disney's outside date of December 17. Among the hired employees is Karandeep Anand, the company's former chief executive, who is now Disney's chief technology officer, as PPC Land reported when Disney paid $20m for Character.ai's IP and $180m for its staff .

# A footnote on personal data
One footnote is new as well: "The Disney Target Assets exclude PII (as defined by section 101(41A) of the Bankruptcy Code)." It restates Disney's position, set out in the company's reply, that it is not buying personally identifiable information and that its agreement should not be reviewed by a consumer privacy ombudsman . A day before the notice was filed, 39 states and DC said Character.ai user data needs a privacy ombudsman to the extent any property that may contain users' personal or "sensitive" information is sold. The footnote uses the narrower statutory term and says nothing about chat content.

# The other changes
The blackline shows four more edits outside the Disney list.

- Wider sale language. The opening paragraph now says the assets will be sold "free and clear of all liens, claims, interest

### 2610.38532v1 pub=2026-10-28T09:39:56Z upd=2026-10-28T09:39:56Z
TITLE: From Leniency to Suspicion: How an Open Post-Training Recipe Changes Whom LLM Fact-Checkers Believe
AUTHORS: Nouar AlDahoul, Yasir Zaki
COMMENT: 10 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Preprint, under review
ABS: LLMs increasingly fact-check online content with the poster's identity in view. However, it remains unclear which post-training changes how much a model's truth judgement depends on the poster's social class, and how such a change happens inside the model. This paper investigates job-based doubt, i.e., judging a claim false more often when the poster has a lower-status job, using fact-checked claims with randomised poster profiles in base and post-trained checkpoints of six model families. Our results reveal that: 1) post-training creates such doubt only with the open Tülu-3 recipe (OLMo-2 32B, Tülu-3 70B), not with Meta's, Alibaba's or Mistral's; the effect is under one percentage point but statistically reliable, exceeding training drift and replicating on independent claim sets; 2) in OLMo-2 32B, the model does not start noticing the poster's job more, but starts interpreting it differently: a lower-status job pushes the base model toward "true" and the post-trained model toward "false"; and 3) this flip is carried by a single residual-stream direction and happens at supervised fine-tuning. The mechanism was confirmed on 400 new claims with pre-specified predictions. None of seven deployed commercial models doubts lower-status posters more. Our work underscores the need to audit speaker bias per training recipe.

### 2610.37685v1 pub=2026-10-14T20:25:40Z upd=2026-10-14T20:25:40Z
TITLE: From Geometry to Behavior: How Instruction Exposure Unlocks Latent Rhetorical Directions in LLMs
AUTHORS: Shengjie Xu
COMMENT: Accepted
ABS: Language models do not merely memorize facts; they absorb rhetorical strategies from pretraining data, including the human tendency to reason by analogy. We ask: is this absorbed capability geometrically accessible before any instruction tuning, and what determines whether it can be activated at inference time? We extract an "Analogy Vector" from the residual stream via difference-in-means and show it enables steerable explanation style across seven instruction-tuned models (Gemma-2, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5; 2B-32B), improving harmonic mean from 3.22 to 3.94 (+22%) for Gemma-2-9B-IT on 300 held-out test prompts. A small human validation study confirms the LLM judge on Analogy Quality. Our central finding, from seven matched base-instruct pairs, is a gradient of behavioral accessibility: the analogy direction exists in every base model, but its behavioral accessibility under linear intervention scales continuously with instruction exposure during training. Gemma-2 base models (strict pretraining/IT separation) show flat steering landscapes: present but behaviorally inert. Qwen-2.5 base models (instruction data woven into pretraining) are already partially accessible before any explicit fine-tuning; base-instruct cosine similarity of the analogy vector reaches 0.94-0.97 for Qwen versus 0.37-0.66 for Gemma, providing geometric corroboration of the behavioral gradient. This challenges the binary "base vs instruct" framing: the relevant variable is how much instruction exposure a model has received across its full training pipeline. We position activation steering as a complementary interpretability tool that reveals how instruction exposure organizes rhetorical knowledge in activation space.

# Chinese Hackers Use AI-Powered ARTEX to Target Over 200 Organizations Worldwide

 Ravie Lakshmanan  Oct 30, 2026 Cyber Espionage / Artificial Intelligence

Chinese state-sponsored threat actors have been observed using a Go-based artificial intelligence (AI)-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX in attacks aimed at high-value targets simultaneously.

The activity has been attributed by CrowdStrike to a China-based "targeted intrusion adversary" it tracks under the moniker Vapor Panda (previously VexatiousTemper). First identified in February 2021, the hacking group overlaps with a threat cluster detailed by Trend Micro as Earth Estries .

"Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission," CrowdStrike said in a Thursday analysis.

Starting October 17, 2026, Vapor Panda is said to have used the AI tool against more than 200 distinct organizations across the world, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions.

Some of the notable targets listed by CrowdStrike are listed below -

- Foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, Central America, and Asia

- A Middle East-based interior ministry

- A European country's foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, along with defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities

- 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors

- Telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines

Post-exploitation activity has been confirmed at nine organizations, allowing the attacker to deploy BLOODALCHEMY , a derivative of ShadowPad, followed by credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance.

Vapor Panda is also said to have conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe.

Central to the operation is the use of ARTEX with DeepSeek and an as-yet-unknown, subscription-based commercial large language model (LLM) to conduct the intrusions at scale, leveraging an army of planner and worker agents that coordinate with each other in pursuit of a common goal to move from initial access to host reconnaissance and lateral movement.

A human operator in the loop oversees the operation, directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and enumerate endpoint sensor coverage.

"In a single intrusion, Vapor Panda's planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole," CrowdStrike said.

Unlike some campaigns that used to assist with individual digital break-ins, the use of ARTEX is at a much higher level to run multiple engagements concurrently, with the human operator only stepping in to steer the agents to accomplish their objective, while taking steps to bypass endpoint defenses.

Analysis of the recovered transcripts highlights the use of ARTEX in combination with tried-and-tested approaches -

- Chaining an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service. This is followed by obtaining a role that can issue administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating access to recover an enterprise administrator account.

- Deploying web shells, abusing an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, reading Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and leveraging resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account.

- Supplying the agent with a set of authentication keys that had not been rotated since 2022, which then uses those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes. In the next phase, the agent uses VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, along with a VPN client key originating from a purported May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network.

"Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure," CrowdStrike explained. "They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations."

The development comes as ARTEX has witnessed broad adoption among threat actors in a short span of time, prompting its developer Li Puhua ("Autumn-27") to take it closed source.

HTTP 200 · https://ppc.land/google-microsoft-openai-and-anthropic-back-one-ai-training-opt-out/ · text/html
Google, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic back one AI training opt-out

Skip to Sidebar
Skip to Content

Search

Google, Microsoft and OpenAI each said on October 30, 2026 that they will honor a single robots.txt instruction that lets a website refuse the use of its content for generative AI training across every participating provider at once, and the Anthropic engineer who wrote the specification told an Internet Engineering Task Force mailing list the same afternoon that his company had already started building support for it.

# In Short
Four big AI companies have agreed to read the same short note on websites that says "do not use my pages to train AI." Until now, a website had to write a separate note for each company's robot, and each company used its own name for that note. The shared note is still a draft, and no company has said it reads it yet: Microsoft starts on February 1, 2027, Google plans to start in early 2027, and OpenAI and Anthropic have not given a date. Microsoft is also retiring its old opt-out method, and at Google the new note will also keep a site out of Gemini answers that cite web pages. Rankings in Google and Bing search results are not affected.

# Four announcements, one mechanism
Google's post, "Supporting a shared AI training control for websites," appeared on the Google Search Central Blog on Friday, October 30, 2026, under the name of John Mueller, Google Search Advocate. Microsoft's Bing Blog published "Your content, your choice: clearer preferences for training and grounding," by Krishna Madhavan, Principal Product Manager, Microsoft Bing, on the same date. OpenAI posted "Making it easier for websites to express AI training preferences" in its Policies and Procedures section, credited to the company rather than to a named author. At 15:39 UTC, Kevin Kelley of Anthropic wrote to the ai-control mailing list of the IETF's AI Preferences working group, known as AIPREF, to say he had submitted a new Internet-Draft, draft-kelley-aipref-training-preference-signal-00.
All four describe the same device. A site operator writes an ordinary robots.txt group, but instead of naming a crawler on the User-Agent line, it names what the draft calls a "policy token." The draft's own illustration reads:
User-Agent: __usage_ai-training
Disallow: /
Allow: /press-kit/

According to the draft, that group "expresses a preference against AI training for all paths except those under /press-kit/, for which it expresses a preference in favor." Lookup follows the path matching and longest-match precedence of RFC 9309, the Robots Exclusion Protocol the IETF published in September 2022.
The rationale was put almost identically by each company. According to Google, website owners will no longer be "managing separate instructions for every AI developer." According to OpenAI, operators previously had to "identify individual crawlers and maintain separate rules for each and every provider." Microsoft described the aim as reducing "the complexity of navigating different platform preferences for the same use of content."
What the four did not share is a start date. Microsoft gave one: it will honor the new preferences from February 1, 2027, as it crawls. Google's blog post says "We aim to support this new control along with other AI providers in 2027," while a note Google added the same day to its crawler documentation is more specific, stating that Google "intends to support the AIPREF shared machine-readable training preference signal (with 'user-agent: __usage_ai-training') in early 2027." OpenAI said it aims "to implement the signal in the coming months." Kelley wrote that Anthropic "has already started implementing support for this draft," without saying when it would be live.

# What the draft actually specifies
The document is short, ten pages including a long acknowledgments table, and its central claim is that it changes nothing about robots.txt itself. "It introduces no new directive names and no new grammar: the path language, longest-match precedence, and group structure of robots.txt are not changed," the abstract says. Kelley is the sole author, listed with an Anthropic affiliation. The draft's intended status is Standards Track, it was last updated on October 30, 2026, and it expires on May 3, 2027.
It lists five goals. Preferences can be bound to individual paths rather than only a whole site. Semantics stay as close as possible to RFC 9309. Expressing a preference should not require restating existing rules, because robots.txt files are size-constrained and "some deployed files already contain heavily duplicated groups." Parsers that do not implement the mechanism should behave exactly as before. And the mechanism "does not depend on the divergent parts of deployed parser behavior."
The token itself, __usage_ai-training , uses only the characters RFC 9309 allows in a product token: letters, underscores and hyphens. Consumers "MUST match policy tokens exactly, apart from case." The double underscore at the front has a practical purpose. According to the draft, "some deployed parsers match more flexibly; the __ prefix makes accidental matches unlikely." A single group may name several policy tokens, and policy tokens may sit in the same group as ordinary crawler names.
Kelley's message explained why the design leans so heavily on existing syntax. "I've spent a lot of time investigating how deployed parsers would interact with a wide variety of ways of expressing preferences in robots.txt files," he wrote. The mechanism, he added, "avoids relying on the areas where deployed parsers behave differently (and let me tell you, there are plenty!)."

# The wildcard rule
One clause will matter more to most site owners than any other. "However, wildcard groups (i.e., User-Agent: *) MUST NOT be interpreted as matching the policy token," the draft states. If no group in a file names __usage_ai-training , "then no preference has been expressed."
The effect is that a site which currently blocks every bot with User-agent: * and Disallow: / has, under the draft, said nothing about AI training. Kelley described this as deliberate. "As a result, a robots.txt file that doesn't use this mechanism, as is true of every one published today, expresses no preference at all," he wrote. Rules addressed to crawler names, and to what the draft calls "proprietary policy tokens" such as Google-Extended , "keep whatever meaning they have today."
The draft also forbids the reverse inference. A consumer that finds only a proprietary token in a file should interpret it as it did before, but "MUST NOT treat it as expressing a preference in the context of this document." A Google-Extended block, in other words, does not count as a shared training opt-out for OpenAI or Microsoft.

# Use, not access
The draft draws a hard line between what a crawler may fetch and what a company may do with the result. "This policy token is not a directive for crawling behavior," it says, and consumers "MUST interpret the RFC 9309 signals being expressed based on their own product token(s) exactly as they would in the absence of this document." Content-usage preferences and traffic management signals "are independent and orthogonal."
That is a direct answer to a gap Google's own staff described nine days earlier. In the second episode of its Non-Canonical Cabinet video series, Google Search Central said robots.txt limits AI crawling, not what bots do with data , calling RFC 9309 an access preference protocol. The policy token is an attempt to carry a statement about use inside the same file.
There is a small but telling gap between the draft and its author's description of it. Kelley wrote that "the draft does ask crawlers not to fetch what they can't use." The text itself is permissive. A consumer that crawls only for purposes covered by the token "MAY refrain from retrieving resources for which a preference against those purposes has been expressed." Under the IETF conventions the draft adopts, MAY marks an option, not a request. A site that wants a crawler to stay away still has to say so in a group for that crawler's own name.

# Precedence, private deals and timing
Three further provisions shape how far the signal reaches. "Specific expressions SHOULD take precedence over general ones," the draft says, and consumers "MAY document that they interpret rules that match proprietary policy tokens as being more specific" than the shared token. Google has done exactly that, as described below.
The second provision concerns licensing. "Private agreements MAY override preferences expressed via this mechanism." A publisher with a content deal can therefore publish a blanket opt-out and still have that deal govern its relationship with a given AI company.
The third concerns time. The draft applies the AIPREF definitions to an "asset," defined as the content retrieved from a path, and states that "the preferences that apply to an asset are those expressed in the robots.txt file in effect when the asset was retrieved." On that wording, a preference attaches to content at the moment of collection. The draft does not address content gathered before a site adds the token.

# What counts as training
The draft does not write its own definition. It takes one from draft-ietf-aipref-vocab-08, "A Vocabulary For Expressing AI Usage Preferences," dated September 13, 2026, by Paul Keller of Open Future and Martin Thomson of Mozilla. AI Training is "Using an asset to modify the learned parameters of a generative AI model."
The exclusions are as important as the definition. Training of models "used to perform exclusively non-generative tasks is not included in this category, even if the model is capable of generative tasks." And a generative AI model, under the vocabulary, "does not include a model that is used, or made available for use, for classification, ranking, or scoring, even where the model generates rationale for its output." Ranking systems of the kind that order search results or score ads fall outside the token on that reading.

HTTP 200 · https://ppc.land/meta-faces-uk-probe-over-planned-terms-to-use-publishers-content-for-ai/ · text/html
Meta faces UK probe over planned terms to use publishers' content for AI

Skip to Sidebar
Skip to Content

Search

The UK's Competition and Markets Authority opened a formal investigation on October 30, 2026 into whether Meta is abusing a dominant position through the commercial terms it sets for businesses that use Facebook, Instagram and its other services. The authority is acting under Chapter II of the Competition Act 1998. Its concern, according to the CMA, is that the terms could allow Meta to collect content from the websites of businesses and publishers that use its services and then use it to develop and provide its own products and services, including its AI features, "without those businesses getting a choice on if or how their content is used."
The revised terms were originally due to take effect on the same day the investigation opened. Meta had already stepped back twice: it moved the effective date to November 20, then announced on October 28 that the rollout would pause while it consulted industry groups. The CMA opened its case regardless. Its case page also reaches further than the press release headline. The investigation will assess whether Meta's "existing commercial terms, or revisions to those terms," amount to an abuse - wording that puts the contract businesses accept now within scope, not only the version that is on hold.

# In Short
Meta wrote new rules for businesses on Facebook and Instagram that could let it take content from their websites and use it for its own products, including AI, with no way to say no. The UK's competition regulator is now investigating whether Meta is so powerful that businesses have no real choice but to accept, and whether pushing such rules on them breaks UK competition law. Meta has paused the new rules, but the investigation goes ahead anyway and can also look at the rules businesses already agree to. Nothing has been decided, and the first round of evidence gathering is scheduled to run until January 2027.

# What the CMA will test
A Chapter II case has two steps, and the CMA has spelled out both. First, the authority will assess whether Meta holds a dominant position in a relevant market in the UK. Only if it finds one does the second question arise: whether the terms amount to an abuse of that position. The two documents published on October 30 phrase the first step slightly differently. The press release refers to "a relevant market"; the case page refers to "one or more relevant markets." Neither names a market. Whether the CMA looks at social media, at display advertising, or at a market built around businesses' access to audiences on Facebook and Instagram is not stated, and that choice will shape everything that follows, because dominance is assessed one market at a time.
The theory of harm is unfair trading conditions . According to the CMA, requiring news publishers and other content businesses to accept the terms "could amount to an unlawful imposition of unfair trading conditions for thousands of UK businesses that rely on its services to reach customers and audiences." The summary at the top of the press release uses sharper language. The CMA, it says, "will examine whether Meta is abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers."
That second group matters. Publishers have led the campaign against the terms since mid-October, but the commercial terms bind every business that runs ads or pages on Meta's platforms, and the CMA's own summary names advertisers alongside publishers. The case page goes broader still, describing the investigation as concerning "Meta's commercial terms for businesses using its platforms and services."
The press release does not use the words crawl, scrape or train. It describes terms that "allow Meta to access and use content from news publishers' websites to develop and provide its own products and services." That is a description of effect, not of method, and it leaves the CMA room to examine the clause however Meta words it in a future version.
Three companies are named as under investigation: Meta Platforms, Inc., Facebook UK Limited and Facebook Ireland Limited. The CMA adds that the investigation "may also concern other entities within Meta's corporate group, including relevant UK subsidiaries."
Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA, framed the case in two paragraphs. "Digital platforms play an important role in helping UK businesses reach millions of customers around the world. But where a company holds a dominant position, it must not use that position to impose unfair terms," she said. "We've heard concerns from news publishers and other businesses and are acting swiftly to investigate whether Meta's proposed changes may breach competition law, using the most appropriate powers available to us to examine these issues in detail. We will be working to reach a swift and satisfactory resolution to this case."
There is a small gap between the two documents here, too. Cardell speaks of "Meta's proposed changes." The case page, the more formal of the two, lists the existing terms first.

# Who brought the complaints
The CMA says it is using its Competition Act powers "so it can urgently investigate the concerns it has heard from stakeholders including the News Media Association and Movement for an Open Web (MOW)."
Movement for an Open Web, an advocacy group whose members include digital advertisers and publishers, said on October 22 that it had complained to both the CMA and the European Commission and had asked for interim measures, Reuters reported that day. Reuters also reported that the CMA had met Meta the day before to get more details on the new business terms. Meta, according to the same report, disagreed with the complaint and said its crawling terms applied only to its ads and business products, that the update did not change how it uses web crawlers, and that content owners could still use robots.txt to signal their preferences.
MOW has taken this route before. It joined the Independent Publishers Alliance's EU antitrust complaint over Google's AI Overviews , filed on June 30, 2025, which also asked for interim measures.
The News Media Association, the UK publishers' trade body, had been explicit about what it wanted from the regulator. On October 23, the day Meta delayed the website-crawling terms to November 20 , its chief executive Theo Bamber called on the CMA to secure public commitments from Meta to drop the offending elements before they took effect and, if Meta refused, to stand ready to begin a strategic market status designation. The CMA has now chosen a different instrument.

# Why competition law, and not the digital markets regime
The explanation sits in the fifth note to editors. "The CMA has limited powers to take action under the digital markets competition regime (DMCR) for businesses that have not been designated with strategic market status. To date, Meta has not been designated with this status under the DMCR," according to the CMA.
The difference is not academic. Under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, a firm with strategic market status can be made subject to conduct requirements without the CMA first proving an abuse. That is the route the authority has taken with Google. The CMA designated Google with strategic market status in general search and search advertising, a designation announced in October 2025, and on June 3, 2026 it used that status to force Google to give publishers controls to keep their content out of AI training and AI Overviews grounding , with the main obligations starting December 3, 2026.
For Meta, that door is not yet open. The CMA says it "continues to keep potential candidates for SMS designation under active review, with the next set of proposals due to be considered by the CMA Board in spring 2027." Even if Meta were among them, a designation would come long after November 20. The Competition Act 1998, by contrast, is available now. Under it, the CMA may open an investigation where it has "reasonable grounds to suspect an infringement of competition law," and the Chapter II prohibition covers conduct by one or more undertakings that amounts to an abuse of a dominant position in a market "and may affect trade within the United Kingdom."
The trade-off is the burden of proof. Instead of setting rules in advance for a designated firm, the CMA must establish dominance and abuse on the evidence, under a procedure that gives Meta the right to respond before any finding is made.

# Interim measures, penalties and the timetable
The Act gives the CMA a faster tool if it wants one. According to its third note to editors, the Competition Act 1998 "also allows for the CMA to impose interim measures where temporary action is needed to prevent significant damage or protect the public interest." That is the power MOW asked for. The CMA's documents mention it but do not say whether the authority has considered using it in this case. Meta's pause means the revised terms are not in force, which is the outcome interim measures are usually sought to secure.
Interim measures against Meta are not hypothetical in Europe. In July 2026, France's competition authority imposed interim measures ordering Meta to negotiate with French press publishers over neighbouring-rights payments, after finding that Meta likely held a dominant position in personal social networking and had likely abused it. On October 29, the day before the CMA announcement, Meta lost its Paris appeal against those measures . The French case concerns different conduct, but it is a recent precedent of a European authority reaching a provisional view that Meta is dominant.
The CMA's documents do not mention financial penalties. Under the Competition Act 1998, an infringement of the Chapter II prohibition can be fined up to 10% of a company's worldwide turnover, the same ceiling that applies under the EU rules. PPC Land's own calculation in an earlier analysis of the fine risk carried by Google's and Meta's new terms put 10% of Meta's 2025 revenue at about $20.10bn. That is a statutory maximum, not an estimate of any outcome, and the CMA is explicit on the point: "At this stage, no assumptions should be made about whether competition law has been broken."
The case page sets out an indicative timetable with two entries:

- October 2026 to January 2027 - rapid initial information gathering and engagement with Meta and third parties

- October 30, 2026 - investigation opened
"The dates above are indicative and may change," according to the CMA. After the initial phase, the authority may close the investigation if it decides not to proceed. If it provisionally considers that competition law has been infringed, it may issue a statement of objections setting out its concerns, and the parties then get an opportunity to respond before a final decision. The case page lists no other route. Cardell's reference to a "swift and satisfactory resolution" leaves open how that resolution might come about.
The CMA has history with Meta under the same Act. Its earlier investigation into Meta's use of data obtained from its advertising customers closed in November 2023 when the authority accepted commitments from Meta, without an infringement finding.
The case team is led by Project Director Tamara Todorovic, with Assistant Project Director Sil van Kordelaar and Senior Responsible Officer Lourenco Ventura. The CMA says anyone with information relevant to the investigation may contact the team.

# How the terms got here
The CMA's press release gives its own account of the dates. "Meta had originally planned to introduce changes to its commercial terms on 30 October but, following active engagement with the CMA, announced that implementation would be delayed until 20 November. Meta has since announced, on 28 October, a pause to the roll out of its commercial terms, pending a consultation with industry groups."

RAID-AI is a free, browser-based ransomware assessment tool for AI systems, created by Behnaz Karimi and Yuvaraj Govindarajulu, the co-leads of OWASP's AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) initiative. Coverage is consistent across sources, with some caveats below.

- **Purpose and origin:** The tool was developed over roughly two years and is described as fully available for anyone to use online for free. Its goal is to help organizations find gaps in their readiness for attacks on AI systems. Karimi has said it targets ransomware against AI systems whether or not the attacker uses AI.
- **Scope:** RAID-AI is a free, browser-based security assessment tool that measures your organization's ransomware resilience specifically for AI systems — mapped to NIST CSF 2.0, CISA CPG 2.0, MITRE ATT&CK, MITRE ATLAS, and NIST Adversarial ML. The vendor page says it covers about 90 controls, including model backups, GPU host hardening, prompt injection defenses, and agentic tool security.
- **Data handling:** According to the project's site, the assessment runs in the browser and stores state locally, so no data leaves the user's machine.
- **Limitations:** The tool is not an automated audit. Results depend on the user's own answers, and it does not verify an organization's security posture independently.
- **Recommended use:** Karimi suggested running it through workshops that bring together security managers, engineers, and AI-security specialists. Govindarajulu and Karimi also ran a Hacktivity workshop on it.

Source notes: The most reliable sources are the Infosecurity Magazine article and the project's own site. A grabify.org page appears to be a republished copy of the Infosecurity article, and a Greek-language AI news digest on GitHub repeats the same facts. I'd treat those two as secondary.

- **Delay:** Meta moved the effective date of its revised Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms from 30 October to 20 November. I couldn't find a report dated October 30, 2026, so this is the best available picture, and the sources conflict.

- **2026 AI-attributed cuts:** One report says AI-linked layoffs reached 87,714, surpassing 2024 and 2025 combined. Another says AI-attributed layoffs in the United States reached 205,000 workers through August 2026. The two figures probably use different methodologies, and I couldn't confirm either from a primary source.
- **Challenger's monthly reporting:** "AI is now the leading reason companies give for cutting jobs," Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas, said in the report.

- **Broader forecasts:** Boston Consulting Group has projected that up to 15% of U.S. jobs could be eliminated over the next five years.
- **Attribution caveat:** A Gartner survey found companies cut jobs over automation whether or not the tech was actually paying off. Treat "AI" as a stated reason, which may not reflect actual automation.

Rebecca Bellan

2:17 PM PDT · October 30, 2026

Investors are getting nervous about AI infrastructure spending just as the Big Tech companies double down.

Over the past two weeks, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft have outlined plans to spend more than $740 billion on capital expenditures this year, which Wall Street is reading as AI infrastructure spending, including data centers and chips.

Earlier in the AI boom, investors largely rewarded such big outlays, viewing them as a sign of confidence in the technology’s growth potential. But as we enter the fourth quarter, that enthusiasm seems to be giving way to concerns about negative free cash flow (spending more cash than a company brings in), mounting debt, and whether these enormous investments will ever generate enough returns.

The anxiety spilled across the market on Friday. The Nasdaq fell 2.9%, and chip stocks took a drubbing, too: Nvidia dropped 4%, Broadcom more than 5%, and Qualcomm 11%. Alphabet, which plummeted 12% on Thursday, its worst day on record, wiping out $500 billion in market value, fell again.

A big part of the concern is that companies that used to have overflowing free cash flow from their core businesses are getting hit as AI threatens the economics of those businesses. Alphabet provided the clearest example of that this week. Google’s parent company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion in the third quarter, its second consecutive quarter in the red, even as quarterly capex grew to $51.4 billion. Alphabet expects to spend up to $205 billion this year, and expects that spending to keep rising in 2027.

DOJ raises privacy concerns over potential sale of Character.AI chats | The Record from Recorded Future News
Image: Getty Images via Unsplash

# DOJ raises privacy concerns over potential sale of Character.AI chats
The Department of Justice is seeking privacy protections for millions of Character.AI customers whose chats and data might be sold as the firm goes through bankruptcy.
The DOJ’s Executive Office for U.S. Trustees said a consumer privacy ombudsman is needed to advise the court on how to regulate what data can be sold and under what terms. The court has the power to restrict the sale of user data, which, in the case of conversations with Character’s chatbots, are often sensitive and sometimes involve minors.
The judge could block the sale of user data held by Character, which DOJ’s bankruptcy office notes has an “ambiguous” privacy policy suggesting it can sell at least some users’ chat histories.
Character is a “first-in-kind super intelligence entertainment platform that allows users to have immersive, multimodal experiences with fictional or imagined characters,” the office said in a Tuesday court filing .
The company currently has 12 million active monthly users worldwide and customers typically spend an average of two hours a day on the platform, according to the filing.
The Character chatbot tells users who ask if their conversations are private that they will not be shared, the filing said.
“Not without your explicit permission,” the filing quotes the chatbot saying. “I’m here as a safe, confidential space to share openly without fear of having it shared elsewhere. I respect your privacy, and I won’t share anything from our conversation unless you give the okay.”
In reality, the Character privacy policy is opaque, the DOJ court filing said, and in some places cautions the AI company may “disclose” personally identifiable information (PII). The policy also says it permits the transfer of PII if the company is sold.
The privacy policy was updated on July 1 while Character was “actively seeking to sell its assets,” the court filing said.
Character should “make a record regarding previous iterations of the policy, including whether it disclosed that transfers of PII may be made during the sale of [Character’s] business or during a reorganization process, how changes were communicated to users, and if [Character] provided sufficient notice of such changes,” according to the filing.
The ombudsman is particularly needed to ensure the sale of sensitive personal content such as minors’ data, health or demographic data or “any information users would reasonably expect to be private is consistent with the privacy policy, any opt outs, and applicable law,” the filing said.
Character.Ai did not respond to a request for comment.

# Private conversations, ‘sellable asset’
People provide chatbots with specific and intimate data which can identify them even if names are removed before data is sold. AI also makes inferring sensitive traits easier, according to Sydney Saubestre, a senior policy analyst focused on privacy and data at the Center for Democracy and Technology.
“Character.AI’s policy reserves the right to disclose user data in connection with a sale of the company or its assets regardless of whether consumers expect their most private conversations to be treated as a sellable asset,” Saubestre said via email.
While the new buyer would be bound by the prior privacy policy, Saubestre said, the buyer can change those practices if consumers consent, which some might do if they are offered incentives. Many people do not realize how easy it is to be identified by detailed chats that occur over several months even when they are purported to be anonymous.
“Users agree to a privacy policy long before anyone contemplates a sale, and that agreement shouldn’t be the only protection for their most private conversations,” she said. “At the very least, customers of the seller should have to opt into the sale of their data to the buyer.”
Personal data is increasingly being used as an asset in bankruptcy sales, including in the March 2025 23andMe bankruptcy case.
Earlier this month, several federal lawmakers sounded the alarm about a pending deal between now defunct Spirit Airlines and Google, which has offered $10 million to the bankrupt airline for reams of employee personal data it wants to use for model training.
At least seven families of users who have committed suicide or suffered mental health harms allegedly due to their use of Character’s chatbot have sued the firm, hastening its financial decline.

HTTP 200 · https://ppc.land/google-and-bing-back-one-robots-txt-rule-to-opt-out-of-ai-training/ · text/html
Google and Bing back one robots.txt rule to opt out of AI training

Skip to Sidebar
Skip to Content

Search

For three years, publishers who wanted to keep their work out of AI training data have had to learn a new crawler name every few months. Google-Extended, GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Applebot-Extended, CCBot: each company built its own switch, and each switch had its own rules about what it covered. On Friday, October 30, the two largest search engines in the Western world said they would honour a single one.
Google said it will voluntarily adopt a proposal under consideration at the Internet Engineering Task Force that lets sites set AI training preferences across several AI providers in a single robots.txt step , Barry Schwartz of Search Engine Roundtable reported. The mechanism is a shared policy token, written in robots.txt as a user-agent called "__usage_ai-training". A site that disallows that token tells every participating company that its content should not be used to train models. "This will help websites express their AI training preferences across multiple AI providers in a single step," Google said in its announcement on the Search Central blog .
The timetable is not immediate. "We aim to support this new control along with other AI providers in 2027, and will provide updates on our progress," Google wrote. Its documentation for common crawlers now says early 2027. John Mueller added a detail that matters for anyone who has already configured Google-Extended: if a site uses the new token to opt out and does not explicitly mention Google-Extended, Google will treat the site as if Google-Extended were disallowed. Existing company-specific controls will keep working, and the opt-out in Search Console remains.
The proposal itself is a draft at the IETF , produced by the AI Preferences working group, known as AIPREF. OpenAI has published its own commitment to the shared signal , and Search Engine Roundtable reported that Anthropic is also participating. Nate Hake, a publisher who has taken part in the working group, cautioned on X that the work is unfinished and some disputes remain unresolved. The difference between a draft and a standard is large. A draft can change wording, scope and syntax before it is adopted, and the companies have committed only to supporting the signal, not to a fixed definition of what training means.
Microsoft went further on the same day. Krishna Madhavan, principal product manager at Bing, announced new Bing AI content controls that separate training from grounding , while keeping eligibility for ordinary search results. Grounding is the process by which an AI assistant retrieves pages at the moment it answers a question, then cites or summarises them. Training is the earlier process of building the model. Until now, most publishers have had to treat them as one decision.
Bing now offers three settings. AI Training allows or prevents use of content to train models. AI Grounding allows or prevents use of content to help generate AI answers. A third option, Limited Grounding, lets a site support Microsoft's own AI products while refusing Microsoft's third-party grounding services, which other companies buy to give their chatbots access to the web. "Microsoft is joining industry peers in announcing a shared AI training preference in robots.txt," the company said, and it is adding page-level training preferences as well. On search rankings, the message was flat: "The traditional Bing rankings are unaffected."
The Bing schedule is precise. From December 15, 2026, temporary grounding controls will appear in Bing Webmaster Tools for sites that use the NoArchive or NoCache directives. From February 1, 2027, Microsoft will begin honouring the new preferences when it crawls. Publishers relying on the old directives have until March 1, 2027 to configure the new ones, and the temporary grounding preferences expire on September 30, 2027. The example Search Engine Roundtable offered was a publisher that blocks training but still lets Copilot cite its articles. The trade-off is explicit: blocking AI answers can reduce visibility in AI experiences.
What the two announcements share is a recognition that the old binary of crawl or do not crawl no longer describes the choices publishers face. What they do not yet share is a common vocabulary beyond training. Google's token covers training alone, while Bing's controls distinguish training from answers. A site that wants to appear in AI Mode citations while staying out of Gemini's training data still has to read two sets of documentation.

# A study puts AI Overviews click-through at 0.9%
The value of appearing in AI answers is the question behind every one of those settings, and new evidence arrived the same morning. Cyrus Shepard published a small case study on LinkedIn in which he used Google's opt-out controls to remove a site from AI Overviews and AI Mode, then compared the traffic before and after. Search Engine Roundtable reported that AI Overviews and AI Mode produced an estimated click-through rate of about 0.9% . "AI impressions had an estimated ~0.9% CTR based on analyzing overall before/after click data (not too shabby)," Shepard wrote.
The finding that drew attention was the second one. When the site was removed from the AI features, its AI impressions fell immediately to zero, as expected. But ordinary organic clicks fell too. Regular organic clicks "ALSO DROPPED when AI features were disabled," Shepard wrote. AI impressions had made up about 8% of the site's total impressions. The URLs with the most AI visibility lost ground and then recovered when visibility was restored. Shepard called the pattern a "Search SERP Halo Effect". Greg Sterling of Near Media suggested in the comments that a presence in AI Overviews seems to create brand lift that leads to later searches and clicks.
Schwartz listed the limits. The sample is one site. AI Overviews still appeared on the results pages during the test; only this site was absent from them. And sitewide average position rose during the period because of new posts and brand searches, which complicates any before-and-after comparison. Still, for publishers weighing the new Google and Bing controls, the study offers a rare measurement of what opting out costs, and it suggests the cost is not limited to the AI features themselves.

# Bing tests ads inside its AI Overviews
Microsoft appears to be testing the commercial side of the same feature. Khushal Bherwani posted a screenshot on X showing a block labelled Sponsored Results inside a Bing AI Overview, and Search Engine Roundtable reported that Bing is showing ads within its Copilot-powered AI Overviews . "Bing is showing Sponsored Results within AI Overviews," Bherwani wrote. Schwartz said he had not seen ads within AI responses on Bing himself and could not trigger them. Microsoft has made no statement.
Bing renamed its Copilot Search box to AI Overviews a few months ago, borrowing Google's term. Placing sponsored results inside the generated summary would bring it closer to Google's model as well, where ads now appear above, below and within AI Overviews in many markets. For Microsoft Advertising, the generated summary is where more queries end, so it is also where the inventory has to be.

# Gemini drops its UTM tags
Measuring visits from AI assistants became harder again. The SEO Natzir found that Gemini stopped attaching UTM parameters to cited links around September 28. Google had begun appending "utm_source=gemini" to citations in early September, a change Search Engine Journal reported at the time . Natzir's chart showed tagged visits growing for three weeks and then vanishing overnight. "Google seems to have stopped appending UTM parameters on Gemini links," Schwartz wrote, adding that he no longer sees them on any Gemini link.
The loss is partial. Visits with a gemini.google.com referrer on the web stayed flat, because the desktop version still passes referrer data. The bigger gap is on phones. Natzir found that Gemini's iOS app opens links in its own embedded browser with no referrer, so those visits land in Google Analytics 4 as Direct traffic. The only trace is a GeminiiOS user-agent in server logs. For marketers trying to size AI referrals, that means some Gemini traffic is invisible to standard analytics and counted as visitors who typed the address themselves.

Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan speaks during a keynote presentation at Computex in Taipei on June 2, 2026.
